title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Whiskerwood
content:
NOTE: This game is currently in Early Access, and this review deals only with the state of the game as it exists in late 2026; when the game is released into 1.0, we may revisit this review.

I’ve previously talked about my abiding love of city-building games in my review of Timberborn, and I am an absolute hog when it comes to games about assembling an increasingly complicated metropolis. In a few ways, Whiskerwood and Timberborn have a lot in common - a citybuilder in a voxel environment with anthropomorphised animal pops, plus verticality and stacking buildings - but while Timberborn is set in the dawning of a post-humanity apocalypse, Whiskerwood takes place in a quasi-17th century world, and while the beavers of Timberborn appear to be entirely alone and isolated in their settlements, masters of all they survey, in Whiskerwood, your “Whiskers” (Mice) are decidedly not.

For you see, the Whiskers of Whiskerwood are colonists, yes, but they are subalterns (in the Gramscian sense) of a greater empire, and, as well as being town planner and resource manager, the player in their role as the chief of these Whiskers (the “Tail”, i.e, you) must function as a sort of intermediary between the oppressed Whiskers and their oppressors, the “Claws” (Cats) and (to a lesser degree) the Weasels. The Claws function as a distant aristocratic overclass, while the Weasels tend towards seafaring renegades, pirates, traders, and smugglers.

From such humble beginnings...

You begin your colony by choosing one of three different starting states. Far Frontier is what you’d call the “standard” game; the state dispatches fewer loyalists, but smugglers demand more goods. Then there's Pirate Seas, which has more pirate ransom requests but tax ships are more infrequent and smuggled goods fetch better prices. Finally, in Monarch Loyalists, the state dispatches far more Monarchist whiskers, and they are willing to tolerate more hardship in general, but are fundamentally anti-industry.

With a scenario selected and a map generated, you can choose a virgin island (the size of which can be altered at the game’s start), abundant in some resources and lacking in others, in a local archipelago and from there, building out your colony the way you’d expect, beginning with access to primitive houses and gathering structures, with a limited get-started packet of resources, so far so normal, this is the ground floor of every colony sim, but what’s this? Two days from now, the Claws will send their envoy for your first.. tax payment? Yes, the cats want taxes from you, and they’re charging you for the supplies you arrived on the island with, plus the costs for the colonists’ passage.

Where the focus of many other citybuilders and colony sims lies on accumulating resources to make your pops happy, to survive the winter, and level up your buildings, in Whiskerwood you’re required to do that while also satisfying the ever-increasing material demands of your feline overlords. Your tax requirement starts on day two and continues every two days, with the exception of Winter, when the cats can’t be bothered to sail to your island (but don’t worry, they’ll add up the tax they don’t take in that time and take it as a lump sum from the survivors when Spring comes, thank-you-very-much).

The way taxes are calculated in Whiskerwood is laid out by the developer, and depends on five variables:

  • Population (a flat rate of 3 coins per day per Whisker)
  • Administrative (13 coins to begin with, increasing by 0.3 for every day survived past the first)
  • Travel (21 coins per colonist ship that turns up)
  • Production (10% of the value of all industrial production)
  • Supply (cost of goods accepted from the supply ship - more on that later).

So, in the absence of some mass die-off event (which can happen; winter is a thing after all), the tax bill is pretty much always going to climb day by day, visit by visit, becoming an increasingly difficult burden to meet as your colony grows.

The logic of colonialism has a high body count

Since the developers of Whiskerwood understand that the primary purpose of a colony in the eye of the parent state is primary sector resource extraction, that is the cats’ sole interest in your case too; although you’ll need to refine resources and manufacture goods and services to keep your whiskers happy and healthy, the cats have absolutely no interest in that nonsense and will not accept any of them as part of a tax payment; in fact, what the cats will accept doesn’t really change throughout the game (with a minor exception), they want logs, they want coal and ores, they want cotton and flax, they want raw fish and berries. Later in the game, when the naval aspect begins to kick off, the cats will add a desire for canvas sails and bronze nails to their list of acceptable payments. Everything else? No, thank you!

This adds an interesting rub to resource management in Whiskerwood. Yes, you need planks for anything more than the most basic construction, and you’ll definitely use them - but if you turn all your logs into the more useful planks, how will you pay your taxes? Do you use the cotton gin to turn your cotton into a superior fabric for making better clothing for your whiskers, or do you save the raw bales for the taxman?

A field to grow cotton

There is, however, a way to use your precious manufactured goods to pay your taxes - the Smuggler. Every once in a while, a smuggler ship will turn up at your dock and offer to buy your manufactured goods in exchange for gold bars, which the cats will accept in payment. Obviously, the smuggler’s prices are not generous (it’s a business, after all), but in a pinch it’s a good way to turn all that excess furniture you have into something you can use to fulfil your obligations to the Claws.

If you’re short on a tax payment, you can still submit it, but the cats’ opinion of you will decrease along a 5-point scale from “happy” to “hostile”, a completely skipped tax payment sees their opinion decrease by 2, a partial payment gives a penalty of 1, while overpaying tax nets a +1 opinion boost (plus a reward), and overpaying tax dramatically gives a +2 opinion boost plus a more generous reward. The rewards for excess tax payments are either one or two selections from a list of various manufactured goods, with different value based on how much you overpaid your taxes. What happens if your opinion slips too far? The tax ships that visit will open fire on your colony, bombarding it with cannonballs for a while before leaving. These bombardments will destroy buildings and pathways, injure, and even kill your Whiskers, making it even harder for your Whiskers to rebuild and be ready for the next tax ship (which is still coming in two days time!). Later in the game, when you’ve got more significant resources, you can construct walls to protect your town from the cannons (since they’re simulated via line of sight from the ship, a bombardment can’t hit a building the ship can’t see), which is also useful against pirates.

Every few days, a ship loaded with supplies will rock up at your main dock and offer you the choice of several packets of resources, typically manufactured goods. These aren’t gifts, though; the cost of whichever packet you select gets added to your next tax bill. You can, of course, refuse to purchase any supply packets, but if you do, you get an immediate -1 opinion malus with the cats for your impertinence. Critically, the Supply Ship and tax-overpayment rewards are the only way to acquire the Machinery resource, required both to build and maintain all factories, but which can’t be produced domestically until the late/end-game.

The Whisker Ship will also visit your dock and offer a range of new colonists you can take on by spending Approval points, either by selecting individuals or accepting the entire shipment at once. As the game is now, Whiskers don’t seem to reproduce, so this is the only way to replace colonists that died of cold, hunger, or bombardment.

Bold (and adorable) sentinels stand ready to face the pirate menace.

Occasionally, a pirate ship will turn up at your dock and demand a ransom, typically in the form of high-quality produced goods like tailored clothes and machinery. Failure to pay results in immediate bombardment by cannon, in the same way as the Claws bombardment. Later in the game, the player can construct anti-pirate defences, like towers armed with cannons that automatically attack approaching pirate ships, along with various quests that include immunity from pirate raids as a reward.

Whiskerwood has an Approval system, whereby the experiences of each Whisker are tallied at the end of each day and assigned a score. Positive experiences like a good meal, warm surroundings, a nice dwelling place, etc. accrue positive points, while unpleasant experiences like homelessness, hunger, unburied bodies, cold, pollution, whether their neighbour snores, bland food, worn-out clothes, an encounter with a rude Whisker, etc. impose a malus on approval. Each of these things is weighed against the expectations of each Whisker (denoted by a star rating on their character card - Whiskers with 1 or half a star will endure pretty severe hardships, eating simple raw fish and living in a hovel without complaining, while a highly skilled or educated Whisker with 4 or 5 stars won’t tolerate anything but the highest standard of living possible, requiring a stone-built house with furniture, bedding, and accessible amenities like a bathhouse and dining hall) and the outcome decides how many approval points you have to spend the next day. Approval points can be spent on a few things, from recruiting new Whiskers, asking workers to perform a double shift, sending a ship to sea, etc. Balancing Approval is one of the trickiest aspects of Whiskerwood; you can’t bank it, you get a fresh amount every day, and the previous day’s approval is lost. Having a high approval but not spending it is pointless, while having low or zero approval can significantly curtail your ability to act. For example, it’s the depths of winter, your Whiskers are all cold and hungry, but you can’t dispatch your Deep Sea Fishing vessel to bring in a large quantity of fish, because launching the ship costs 20 approval and you’ve not got any!

Summary of Day #523's production, consumption, approval, and taxes

To produce the end-game resources your high-status Whiskers crave, you’ll often need to manage considerably more complicated supply chains - for example, to produce a high-quality meal, you’ll need to catch fish, grow wheat, grow peppers, and grow mushrooms; you’ll then need to process that wheat into flour in a windmill, then turn that flour into bread in a bakery. You’ll need to combine the fish with fuel and mushrooms at a smokery to turn it into a fish skewer; you’ll also need to grind peppers into spices and combine all three things- bread, skewer, and spices at a Fine Kitchen building, staffed by a Craftmaster and two Educated Whiskers. To improve this production, you can add table salt as a catalyst, which is produced by mining rock salt and passing it through a sifting tower (which requires piped water from a pumping station). That’s a pretty complicated process to make a meal, but it’s what your higher-status Whiskers will demand!

Monarchist Whiskers are a particular pain in the arse, complaining about the presence of factories being an affront to the generosity of the Claws. Even among the oppressed, there are always those who love the oppressor.

Since this is a colony sim, your main enemy is always going to be Winter. Even though the islands look pretty warm, when the dark season rolls around, temperatures plunge into the single digits and Whiskers will start to sicken and die if they aren’t kept warm. To that end, you need to build bonfires, heating stoves, and later Steam Radiators to warm the surrounding environment and make life possible in the depths of the snowy winter (and also to prevent farm ground from freezing and being unavailable all winter), but each of these methods both uses fuel and generates pollution. Later-game heating like the aforementioned Steam Radiators generate significantly less pollution (and since the steam travels from the boiler to the radiator through pipes, it’s possible to have the pollution-emitting aspect further away from where people actually live) but have an increased material cost to build; you need a lot of copper available to build the boilers and pipes to run the radiators, and to unlock the technology in the first place. So in the earlier game, your Whiskers will either be freezing in winter or complaining bitterly about the pollution produced by the bonfires keeping them alive, typical.

The slice view enables you to excavate huge caverns for farming mushrooms and digging up ores and stone

Each Whisker is automatically assigned to a particular guild from a list of four: Miners, Engineers, Farmers, and Explorers - being assigned to a job that matches their guild affiliation gives an associated productivity boost, and having all workers in a particular workplace have the same guild affiliation adds another boost. In addition, each Whisker can have advanced vocational or educational traits enabling them to take on more advanced jobs. An Apprentice is a worker with a basic level of additional vocational education. In a lot of factories, the first worker must be an Apprentice, and if none are available, the factory won’t function at all. To begin with, the only way to get an Apprentice is if one turns up to your colony on a Whisker Ship, but once you have Whiskers with advanced educational traits, you can employ them at a School and, through doing so, give additional Whiskers their education trait or guild affiliation.

Both workers on this cotton farm are in the Farmer's Guild, so they get a speed bonus.

Beware, though, if you’re thinking “I would just set up schools to educate all of my Whiskers to Apprentice level”, Whiskers with advanced education will have a higher expectation ranking and will be much more demanding when it comes to creature comforts! Beyond Apprentice, you can train Whiskers as Craftmasters, Educated, and as Sailors. Craftmasters are the most elite of the manual workers, and are often required to fill the last position in a factory and provide a significant boost to production by their presence. In some late–game factories like the Machinist, the only acceptable employees are Craftmasters, so keeping track of where your elite labourers are assigned is key to an efficient colony - having an Engineer's Guild Craftmaster working an unskilled job growing Flax while your Machinist goes unstaffed and there are unskilled Farmer’s Guild Whiskers hanging around unemployed is no good for the collective.

At least one Whisker with the Sailor trait is required to staff a ship - that doesn’t mean all the workers on a ship must be sailors (though there’s a production boost if they are).

Educated Whiskers are required to fulfil the need for bureaucrats, researchers, and producers of science-y things like chemicals and medicines.

This institution of classes even among the subaltern colonists is interesting; even effective slaves can live a somewhat bourgeois life, living in comfortable, warm housing replete with furniture and bedding, eating nice meals and engaging in activities like visiting a bathhouse. Lower-status Whiskers are not banned from enjoying these creature comforts, and will greatly appreciate them, but your educated and skilled workers will expect them and be deeply unhappy if you fail to provide (and they'll let you know via a big Approval penalty).

Later in the game, you can research and construct adorable railway systems to improve transit around your colony

Research in Whiskerwood takes the typical form of tech-trees unlocked by the spending of resources. You build a Research Lab, staff it with educated Whiskers, choose which technology/building you want them to work on, and they consume the necessary resources until the tech is unlocked. Each tech either enables the creation of a new building or unlocks an additional recipe for an existing factory (e.g, enabling the Ore Furnace to produce Bronze as well as Copper). You can build additional Research Labs, but Whiskerwood discourages speedrunning the tech tree by introducing a production malus on every research lab for every additional one you build (called Coordination). It’s still faster to have two (or more) Research Labs than one, but it is not 2x faster, more like 1.7x faster, decreasing with every additional lab built.

As of the time of writing, the endgame - which I presume involves boosting your military capability, declaring independence, and fighting the Claws to secure it is not yet entirely implemented, but will probably include more extensive defensive buildings and naval combat. At present, you can construct naval vessels and dispatch fleets to reduce Pirate islands, but at the moment the quests seem to be bugged, in that you can just repeat the pirate quests constantly and receive so many days of immunity that pirates cease to be an issue altogether. I expect that in the full release the naval aspect of the game will be considerably tweaked and expanded, but I certainly can’t say for sure.

Whiskerwood is a great game with enough complexity to scratch the citybuilder itch, and although it peters out a bit at the endgame as your industry becomes strong enough that your whiskers produce wealth and abundance far beyond the tax bill, this is pretty normal for Early Access games that aren’t technically “finished” yet. It’s not unreasonable to frontload development into ensuring that the early and midgame are more polished as a sort of “setting out the stall” exercise to intrigue interested buyers - a lot of early access games morph significantly during their development (Timberborn is vastly more polished now than it was when the Early Access was floated), and I certainly don’t begrudge the studio for this approach; I can’t wait to play full-fat 1.0 whenever it turns up.

If you love Timberborn, but wish it was a bit more like Anno, you’ll certainly love this, and if you like citybuilders in general, the Whiskerwood experience is well worth your time.

title: MTG Nauctis has whale gods, elemental krakens, and a new 'Black Lotus'
content:
Wizards of the Coast revealed details, art, and a couple of card spoilers for the first MTG set of 2027: Nauctis.

They teased their new evasive mechanic 'dive', brought back Descent, and told us about different creature types and their color identities. But more importantly, we got to learn about MTG Nauctis' gods.

While we only saw one at the show, Nauctis has a complete cycle of whale gods. It's only fitting that the largest creature on earth fulfils this role in the undersea plane. Salinae, the Ocean Mother gets cheaper based on your devotion to blue and makes 1/1 fish copies of every artifact or creature you cast.

While blue, green, and white whales appear in the set proper, the red and black ones are consigned to the commander decks. Taking their place in this mythic cycle are two sinister elemental krakens. One remains unspoiled, but Tecton, Malignant Horror may be my favorite visual design from the set, a huge tentacle monster made of whale skeletons. The effect is pretty straightforward actually: you draw a card when you sacrifice anything. Seems like it'd be good with blood or treasure tokens.

Here's what we learned about the creatures of Nauctis, and the archetypes they fill:

Seals are red and white aggro - the Nauctis equivalent of dwarves, they're skilled crafters.

There are two kinds of sharks: shark people are blue-red pirates while bestial shark creatures are red green. Goramou of the Coral-Taken is an example of the latter. She looks terrifying, but just wants to help you ramp.

Finally, we heard about the merfolk, who are in Bant in this set, found in blue, white, and green. They are central to the story, an ancient ruling culture affected by a schism around an independent city state.

Finally, we saw Nauctis' headliner card, which is Abyssal Lotus. It's a much less broken take on Black Lotus, which works just like the famous Power 9 piece, but firstly it only works if there are eight or more permanents in the graveyard, and it enters tapped (boo). Still, it's likely to be the expensive card of the set, especially the ultra-rare textless version.

Share your thoughts on the set at the Wargamer Discord.

title: [40k] Big Hat, Reviewed
content:
The hat, she is big. Specifically, I am posting from within the 1:1 scale Mark X helmet (in Dark Angels colors, necessarily) from Joy Toy. I paid my own money for it, and got the one with the stand and the included t-shirt.

The author, pictured. Credit: Greg Chiasson

As an aside, it is not lost on me that the only two articles I’ve written since my son was born have been about 1. sitting in a comfy chair and 2. wearing a dorky hat. I realize how this looks, but I don't generally buy things. I do, obviously, but only when forced. I cycle through two water bottles, and both have my company's logo on them. My main hoodie is also something I got for free. I haven't spent my own money on a computer since 2014, and only last year got a new phone, getting rid of an iPhone that was fully a decade old. So the fact that I've been instantly and furiously slamming the buy button on any Warhammer merch with a Dark Angel on it represents either intense personal growth or whatever the opposite of growth is.

Take a quick peek at this photo, and think about how your head would fit in there. Wrong, it’s bigger. Roomier. Cavernous. This helmet is enormous on a replacement-size human, but comically tiny on an Intercessor model, which really drives home how massive a Space Marine must be. This information may not rise to the level of useful, but it is at a minimum illustrative.

The big hat existed already, in an Ultramarines version. Many of us have purchased it, talked about it, and perhaps even reviewed it. If we did the latter, I haven’t read it, and you shouldn’t either. I will explain why: the Ultras version could not have been better than a 4 out of 5, because this is a 5 out of 5 and if painted as any other chapter it could - objectively - not be rated as highly. Equally, it could not have been worse than a 4 out of 5, because it is, at the end of the day, still a big goofy space helmet you can wear around your home, and categorically that cannot be a bad thing. So that review, if it exists, is not required reading; it either ends the way I already told you it does and your curiosity is now sated, or it doesn’t and is thus so wrongheaded in its conclusion that you can skip it.

I mentioned that the helmet comes with a stand and a Dark Angels shirt. The shirt absolutely whips; great design, is appropriately Dark Angelic, and better quality material than I’d expect, given the source.

The stand looks like nothing so much as an oversized piece of Warhammer terrain, which I mean as a compliment. The Dark Angels logo on the front is a separate piece, which makes sense if they wanted to use the same stand design for other, lesser, chapters.

It does feel like the Warhammer merch people are making up bullshit directly for me, and to them I would say: keep it up, I have poor impulse control. Lest you think that’s a joke, I want to point out that when the Dark Angels chapter banner went up for pre-order, there was a gap of less than two minutes between Rob sending me the link and me replying with a screenshot of my order confirmation. I know what I’m about here.

Much like that banner, I still don’t know where to put this gigantic thing. For now, it lives on top of my printer, and so every time I want to print anything I have to move it out of the way or it causes a paper jam. Admittedly that problem is specific to me, but otherwise: what is it like living with big hat? How practical of a wardrobe or lifestyle choice is it? In terms of the five main senses - I don’t have any proven psychic or psionic abilities, but I assume the helmet wouldn’t interfere with those, and it’s plastic so something like an electric Eel, or a direction-finding organ attuned to the earth’s magnetic field, should be fine - the results are surprisingly positive.

Sight: I watched some of Dune Part 2. The tinted eye lenses turn everything red, which is a problem generally speaking but notably makes the Giedi Prime gladiator sequence look insanely cool. This was all aided by the fact that it’s roomy enough in there that I could keep my glasses on the entire time. That said, the big hat does have a limited field of view, so if/when I go to an IMAX showing of Dune Part 3, I will probably not wear this.

Insanely cool to watch Dune through a Dark Angels hat.

Sound: Phoebe Bridgers’ Lost Weekend is a towering achievement, an absolutely titanic record. I don’t want to be reductive about this, because it’s a very good album that can’t be filed away or derided as sad music about boys - it’s weird and incisive and will probably rewire my brain the same way that Punisher did - but some portion of it is about her relationship with Bo Burnham, and a lot of the rest is about her relationship with her (dead? I should look that up) father. Now, as also the father of a daughter, if my kid grows up and writes an album this good, but where she talks about me like that, I would be very proud of her and also probably want to fake my own death to get away from it.

Anyway I can’t hear things very well through the helmet. The muffling effect is pronounced, and when music isn’t playing, it makes my tinnitus go hog wild.

Touch: You cannot be touched while wearing this, which is bad. However, that is what helmets are for, which is good. So this test fails, but fails by design, and so paradoxically it passes.

For the helmet’s part, where it touches the top of your head there’s an adjustable doodad that keeps it steady and comfortable. No complaints, really.

Taste: There is enough room to sneak a hand up in there and eat a small snack without taking the big hat off your head, but something like a pulled pork or even brisket sandwich would not fit. A popsicle or corn dog shape would probably work. Nothing bigger than that though.

Smell: There’s no nose hole up front, but the neck hole on the bottom is gigantic, so you can position your behelmed head above the Dark Angels scented candle and still get a whiff of whatever they were trying to do there.

I love the big hat, for some of the same reasons that I love the chair. No, this one isn’t nearly as useful, but it still amuses me that it exists, and I enjoy having it in my presence. I am going to go on claiming to be god’s only creation that is immune to propaganda, but I think we can look at the fact that I spent two hundred dollars on something to take up space I don’t have just because it was the right shade of green, and know on some level that I am lying. The trade-off for chaining myself to samsara a bit more tightly is that I can sit in my Dark Angels chair, wearing my Dark Angels shirt and helmet, looking at my Dark Angels art prints and painted models and (soon enough) anime wall-scroll banner, and feel incredibly, unspeakably, Normal. The feeling won’t last, but as long as they keep putting out new Dark Angels merch to distract me from reality I can skip from purchase to purchase like a stone across a pond and never have to confront anything. The stupider the better.

title: Pokémon Pocket lost 9 million users and 60% profit in the last year
content:
DeNA has reported its quarterly financial results, and it shows a continued pattern since early 2025 of fans gradually abandoning its hit TCG app Pokémon Pocket.

According to the results, which were published November 10, the revenue of the game business segment was down 28.8% year-on-year, while profits took a more significant tumble, down 60%. Now, in fairness, that's still $42 million profit, hardly something to cry about, but it does show that fans are continuing to bleed away from Pocket, despite all the app's new sets and changes.

In fact, a Q&A with shareholders revealed that monthly active users were down to 21 million in Q2, way less than the 30 million who were playing this time last year.

The company promised "additional initiatives and efforts" to help Pokémon Pocket recover its momentum, and pointed out that key metrics were starting to stabilize.

That's a reasonable point. The drop in players has definitely slowed down significantly in recent months. For instance, MAU dropped from 39 million in Q1 2025 to 30 million in Q2 2025. But between the first two quarters of this year it only fell by 2 million, from 23 million to 21.

We'll be interested to see what happens next, if the game continues to recover momentum this fall.

Let us know if you're still playing Pokémon Pocket? I got locked out last year when upgrading phones and never took the time to recover my account.

title: All Legendary Pokémon and Mythical Pokémon in order
content:
Legendary Pokémon are iconic - they have the most elaborate designs, the best stats, and some of the mightiest Pokémon cards. While all Mythical and Legendary Pokémon were once few in number, each new game has added more. To help you keep track, we've created this handy list of all 71 Legendaries and 23 Mythicals you can catch or collect.

If you'd like a complete Legendary and Mythical Pokémon list, this guide can provide - but our full 'How many Pokémon are there?' guide covers pocket monsters of all kinds. If you like rare and powerful things, you might also be interested in our guides to rare Pokémon cards. For now, though, let's meet the legends.

Gen 1 Legendary Pokémon

NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Articuno#144Ice/Flying485
Zapdos#145Electric/Flying490
Moltres#146Fire/Flying495
Mewtwo#150Psychic590

In Pokémon Red and Blue, Mewtwo was an end-game secret. It appears in the high-level Cerulean Cave, which can only be accessed after beating the Elite Four and winning the Pokémon League.

In the English language version of Pokèmon, Articuno, Zapdos, and Moltres have names that end in the Spanish words for one, two, and three. Their Japanese names are a lot more descriptive: フリーザー (Furiizaa), aka Freezer; サンダー (Sandaa), aka Thunder; and ファイヤー(Faiyaa), aka Fire.

Gen 1 Mythical Pokémon

 NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Mew#151Psychic500

Mew was never intended to be a publicly available Pokémon. Developer Shigeki Morimoto added Mew to the code as an Easter egg just for his colleagues at Game Freak, using space on the cartridge that was freed up after debug tools were removed. Some players discovered Mew via glitches, starting rumors of a secret Pokémon that were hard for fans to verify or disprove in the early days of the internet.

The first time players could legitimately catch Mew was in Spring 1996, when Game Freak ran a promotion in manga magazine CoroCoro Comic, offering a few lucky winners the chance to mail in their game cartridge to have Mew added to their Pokédex.

How rare is Mew?

In the world of Pokémon, there is only one Mew. According to the events of Pokémon: The First Movie, Mew is an ancient species of Pokémon long thought extinct.

Mew is generally only available during special events. For example, in September 2023, it was possible to use a Mystery Gift and a code to unlock Mew in Pokemon Scarlet and Violet - but that code has since expired. However, it is available in Pokémon Brilliant Diamond and Shining Pearl if you have save data from Pokémon: Let's Go, Pikachu! or Let's Go: Eevee! on your Switch.

Gen 2 Legendary Pokémon

NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Raikou#243Electric580
Entei#244Fire580
Suicune#245Water580
Lugia#249Psychic/Flying680
Ho-Oh#250Fire/Flying680

Four-legged counterparts to the Legendary birds, Raikou, Entei, and Suicune were the games' first 'roaming Pokémon'. Instead of appearing as static encounters, they could be found out in the world.

Ho-Oh was the 152nd Pokémon ever revealed, and the first sign that The Pokémon Company planned to expand beyond the original 151.

Not only was Ho-Oh teased in the CoroCoro magazine, but it also made an appearance in the very first episode of the Pokémon anime. Protagonist Ash Ketchum spots a Ho-Oh, but his Pokédex is unable to identify it.

Lugia is a lead character in the second Pokémon movie 'The Power of One', the leader of the Legendary birds, and the only one who is able to stop their squabbling.

Gen 2 Mythical Pokémon

NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Celebi#251Psychic/Grass600

When the time came for the Pokémon Company to make follow-ups to its unexpected global smash hit game, it had a much better idea of what kinds of things would be popular with fans - and it was determined to repeat the success of the mythical Mew. Enter Celebi, which, unlike its forebear, was planned for in advance.

Which isn't to say it was much easier to get Celebi, at least not in the original release. The critter would only spawn if the player acquired a Great Smith's Ball. Not only was this item only available during a special event, you needed to use the rudimentary cell data transfer from the Game Boy Color's 'Game Boy Mobile' peripheral - something that was only available for the Japanese version of the handheld!

Did you know? Sprites from a datamined beta version of Gold and Silver seem to show this Pokémon originally started out as something closely resembling a depiction of Kokopelli, a Native American fertility deity. It ended up being worked into a very different kind of creature, although Celebi still makes the plants grow.

Gen 3 Legendary Pokémon

NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Regirock#377Rock580
Regice#378Ice580
Registeel#379Steel580
Latias#380Dragon/Psychic600
Latios#381Dragon/Psychic600
Kyogre#382Water670
Groudon#383Ground670
Rayquaza#384Dragon/Flying680

Rayquaza has the highest base Attack, Special Attack, and the highest total of all base stats, of any Dragon-type or Flying-type Pokémon - but it has sometimes been very easy to catch.

In Pokémon Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire, Rayquaza was needed to progress the Delta Episode side plot. The developers changed its catch rate from 3 to 45 (higher means easier, so this was a huge change) to ensure players would be able to snatch up the big green noodle. This was reverted in Scarlet and Violet when the mighty dragon reappeared in The Hidden Treasure of Area Zero.

Regice, Regirock, and Registeel, also called the Giants of Legend, are some of the trickiest Legendary Pokémon to find in the games. In Ruby, Sapphire, or Emerald, you have to translate braille and then do a bunch of puzzles to unlock them.

Latios and Latias are, effectively, the same species, with Latios being male and Latias being female - just like the male and female Nidoran evolutionary line.

Kyogre is one of many Legendary Pokémon we're labeling as a 'potential apocalypse'. It has the ability to control the level of the oceans, and is believed by some to be the creator of the oceans in primordial times. In Pokémon Sapphire and Emerald, team Aqua has the very normal goal of finding Kyogre and using it to raise the sea levels to create more homes for aquatic Pokémon (never mind how many countries get flooded in the process!).

Groudon and Kyogre famously don't get on, as the former is said to have fallen into a long slumber after an apocalyptic battle with the latter. Perhaps it's because Groudon is, in myth, considered to be responsible for creating continents. Land and sea are just too different, it seems.

Gen 3 Mythical Pokémon

NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Jirachi#385Steel/Psychic600
Deoxys#386Psychic600

Jirachi is a bit like a mythical genie, a Pokémon that sleeps for a thousand years at a time before waking up to grant three wishes. While all the anime stories about Jirachi centre on this wish-granting ability - and what happens when people abuse it - in game, it stands out for a very different reason. It's the only Pokémon capable of learning the move Doom Desire, a damage dealing Steel type move.

Is Deoxys even a Pokémon, when it evolved from an extra-terrestrial virus? It's in the Pokédex, so we guess it still counts. This strange Pokémon does not evolve, but it can change between four Formes by being exposed to different meteorites: Normal Forme, Attack Forme, Defense Forme, and Speed Forme. And it has another ability that has never appeared in a game: in the comics it's capable of creating clones of itself!

Gen 4 Legendary Pokémon

NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Uxie#480Psychic580
Mesprit#481Psychic580
Azelf#482Psychic580
Dialga#483Steel/Dragon680
Palkia#484Water/Dragon680
Heatran#485Fire/Steel600
Regigigas#486Normal670
Giratina#487Ghost/Dragon680
Cresselia#488Psychic600

The Legendary Pokémon that appeared in Pokémon Diamond and Pearl really push the power level for the franchise. Dialga has the ability to control time, Palkia can warp space, and together they are capable of creating new universes.

Meanwhile, Giratina can rip holes in reality and lurks in the Distortion dimension. Many fans think of him as Pokémon's equivalent of the devil.

Uxie, Mesprit, and Azelf are the three Lake Guardians of the Sinnoh region. Their Pokédex entries reveal they are associated with knowledge, emotion, and willpower respectively. This is a reference to the 'three sacred treasures' of Japan, artifacts that belong to the Imperial Japanese household and can be traced back to ancient myth - a mirror that represents wisdom, a jewel that represents benevolence, and a sword that represents valor.

Heatran is believed to be the physical embodiment of the planet's core. It would apparently go on a magma-fueled rampage if a Magma Stone didn't keep it sealed in a volcanic crater. So, you know, it's the perfect companion for a 10-year-old Pokémon trainer.

Cresselia has slightly more chill. This ethereal lunar Pokémon specializes in healing, and its feathers even give someone who holds it pleasant dreams.

On both ends of the 'chill vs not chill' scale is Regigigas, a Pokémon with far too many Gs in its name. This legendary is credited with creating a legion of other legendary giants. While it can be calm and thoughtful, Regigigas can also cause immense devastation when rampaging - and has the power to override the authority of any puny human who might think they control one of Regigigas' creations.

Gen 4 Mythical Pokémon

NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Phione#489Water480
Manaphy#490Water600
Darkrai#491Dark600
Shaymin#492Grass600
Arceus#493Normal720

Arceus is perhaps the most powerful Mythical Pokémon. It's worshiped as a deity by some humans, who may actually be right - it could be the creator of the Pokémon universe.

On the less powerful side is Darkrai, who is apparently harmless but likes to keep people away by inflicting them with horrific nightmares. These can be stopped with a feather from Darkrai's lunar counterpart, the Legendary Pokémon Cresselia.

Shaymin saw everyone calling Mew adorable and said 'hold my drink'. This shy cutiepie avoids interacting with others by disguising itself as a flower, and its petals are capable of absorbing toxins and pollution.

Manaphy is an unusual Mythical Pokémon, not just because it's inspired by the colorful slugs known as sea angels, but also because it's capable of breeding. Because its gender is unknown, Manaphy can only breed with Ditto. When this happens, it produces a Phione!

Gen 5 Legendary Pokémon

NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Cobalion#638Steel/Fighting580
Terrakion#639Rock/Fighting580
Virizion#640Grass/Fighting580
Tornadus#641Flying580
Thundurus#642Electric/Flying580

Zekrom#644Dragon/Electric680
Landorus#645Ground/Flying600
Kyurem#646Dragon/Ice660

Known as the 'Swords of Justice', the three Fighting type Legendaries Cobalion, Terrakion,and Virizion are inspired by the Three Musketeers. Which makes it a bit strange that they appeared in Generation five, and not the France-inspired region Kalos in Generation six!

Thundurus, Landorus, and Tornadus are collectively known as the 'Forces of Nature' and would be joined by a fourth member, Enamorus, a couple of generations later. These Pokémon have almost identical 'incarnate' forms, but each one also has a more animalistic 'therian' form which sets it apart and changes its stats.

Tornadus also has the honor of being the first pure Flying type Pokémon, indicating that it's not just a creature that flies, but an elemental intrinsically connected with air.

Nicknamed the 'Tao trio' by fans, Reshiram, Zekrom, and Kyurem are all prevalent mythological creatures in the Unova region. Reshiram has potentially world-ending fire powers and a serious commitment to truth, while Zekrom has potentially world-ending lightning powers and a dedication to noble ideas.

Kyurem has a strange relationship to the other pair - this extra-terrestrial Pokémon can perform an 'absofusion' with either Reshiram or Zekrom using a DNA Splicer, becoming White Kyurem or Black Kyurem respectively. The process can be undone using the DNA Splicers again, so this isn't a situation where you need to trade with a buddy to complete this part of your Pokédex.

Gen 5 Mythical Pokémon

NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Victini#494Psychic/Fire600
Keldeo#647Water/Fighting580
Meloetta#648Normal/Psychic or Normal/Fighting600
Genesect#649Bug/Steel600

Victini has a unique gimmick. Whereas most Legendary and Mythical Pokémon show up at the end of the Pokédex, this is the first Unovan Pokémon - with National Dex Number #000.

There's some in-game dialogue about that number letting it 'bring victory' to the holder of the 'dex, but it's not very convincing: more likely, the designers just wanted to mark it out as special.

Keldeo is actually the adopted ward of the three Swords of Justice, who took the poor 'lil pony in after a fire separated it from its parents. That's the saddest backstory we've heard since the days of Cubone.

Meloetta actually has two formes, Aria forme - a Normal / Psychic type Pokémon - and Pirhouette forme, which is Normal / Fighting type. Aria forme is how you will first encounter Meloetta, and it needs to learn the unique move Relic Song before it can transform for the duration of a battle.

Genesect is a man-made Mythical Pokémon. A sort of robot counterpart to Mewtwo, it was resurrected from a fossil and then modified by the evil Team Plasma. Genesect's signature move Techno Blast changes type depending on the item you give to this Pokémon.

Gen 6 Legendary Pokémon

NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Xerneas#716Fairy680
Yveltal#717Dark/Flying680
Zygarde#718Dragon/Ground600

These three Legendary Pokémon are known as the Aura Trio by fans. They obviously resemble the letters X, Y, and Z, but are often theorized to be inspired by creatures from Celtic or Norse mythology as well, with Zygarde in particular being linked to the World Serpent Jormungandr.

Zygarde's appearance changed considerably between its first appearance in Gen 6 and its return in Gen 7.  On its first appearance, it had only its scaly, slithery appearance - but when it returned it had three 'Formes'.

See, Zygarde is actually composed of multiple components: the sentient Zygarde Cores that control its behavior, and the non-sentient Zygarde Cells that make up its body. Depending on how many of these are gathered together, it can appear as a hound-like 10% Forme, the serpentine 50% Forme, and a Power-Rangers-style Complete Forme.

Xerneas' form transformation is much less dramatic. This deerlike Pokémon spends most of its time in Normal mode, and when it transforms into Active mode its antlers and the go-faster stripes on its legs glow. In this mode it has the power to bestow eternal life, but it also looks like a Christmas decoration.

Xerneas is tasked with overseeing the balance between life and death along with its counterpart Yveltal, the physical embodiment of death and destruction. This Pokémon absorbs the life of other creatures to survive, which is very metal, but we think this is one we'd deposit in the Pokébank and leave there.

Gen 6 Mythical Pokémon

NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Diancie#719Rock/Fairy600
Hoopa#720Psychic/Ghost600
Volcanion#721Fire/Water600

The Mythical Pokémon Volcanion was the first Fire and Water type ever created, and three generations later, it's still the only one in the game. Which is a shame, as it's a pretty sweet type combo, with three 4x resistances.

In fact, all three of Gen 6's Mythicals broke new ground in terms of typing. Diancie is a very rare Rock / Fairy type, a status it shares with Carbink - technically it's a mutation of that much less rare 'mon. Then Hoopa is the first Psychic / Ghost type.

The four Tapu Pokémon - Tapu Koko, Tapu Lele, Tapu Bulu, and Tapu Fini - are guardian deities of the four islands that make up the Alola region. While most Legendary Pokémon are pretty loose in their ties to real-world mythology or religion, these four are quite clearly inspired by the four great gods of Hawaiian religion. Each has a 'shell' it can close up to form a stylized animal head.

Cosmog is a very unusual Legendary Pokémon, as it has an evolutionary line. First it becomes the massive Cosmoem, which is tied with Celesteela as the heaviest Pokémon, weighing in at a chunky 999.9kg. In the anime, Ash Ketchum carries the colossal weight around effortlessly, so I guess we can add super-strength to the boy's list of superpowers, right next to 'never ageing'.

Cosmoem can then evolve into two different Legendaries, Solgaleo and Lunala, which are conspicuously styled after the sun and moon respectively.

Cosmog's stablemate Type: Null is another evolving Legendary Pokémon, thought its line is considerably shorter - it caps out once it evolves into Silvally. It's a chimera created from cells from every known Pokémon, and was intended to fight against the dimension-leaping Ultra Beasts.

Gen 7 Mythical Pokémon

NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Magearna#801Steel/Fairy600
Marshadow#802Fighting/Ghost600
Zeraora#807Electric600
Meltan#808Steel300
Melmetal#809Steel600

Generation 7 really went overboard with the Mythical Pokémon, with a whopping five of them in total! And some have multiple forms they can take.

For instance, the clockwork Magearna has a basic silver form, and a painted Original Color variant with gold metallics and a red and white dress designed to look like a Pokéball. This aesthetic is also reflected in the Pokémon's Mega Evolution form, which turbo-charges its special attack.

Marshadow stands out thanks to its awesome Ghost/Fighting typing, and its spooky, shadowy appearance. Unusually, this Pokémon's shiny looks completely identical to the regular version. The difference is only noticeable when it enters its Zenith form, which activates on certain attacks. Like Magearna, the different is purely an aesthetic one, and doesn't have any gameplay effect - but it does make it a nightmare for shiny hunters to catch!

Zeraora is actually the first Mythical Pokémon with the Electric type. Impressive to be a first so late in this game's life! In Pokémon Legends Z to A's Mega Dimension DLC, this Pokémon received a new Mega form which gives it a snazzy black and blue coloration, and the highest attack stat of any electric type. It's also the fastest Mega Evolution!

Meltan and Melmetal are Mythical Pokémon that made their first appearance in the app Pokémon GO, which is still just about the only way to get them - though they can be imported to the console games Let's Go Pikachu and Let's Go Eevee via the GO Park, and Pokémon Sword and Shield via Pokémon Home.

Gen 8 Legendary Pokémon

Zacian#888Fairy670/

Enamorus#899Fairy/Flying580

Zacian and Zamazenta are best known in their Crowned Shield/Sword forms, which they transform into when given special items to hold. They then gain an additional Steel typing, as well as a sizeable stat boost.

Not counting Dynamax and Gigantamax Pokémon, Eternatus is the tallest known Pokémon. It's actually the source of the Dynamax phenomenon that causes Pokémon to temporarily turn gigantic in the Galar region in Pokémon Sword and Shield.

On the smaller side is Kubfu, an adorable 'lil martial arts bear that evolves into one of two different types of Urshifu (Fighting/Water or Fighting/Dark) depending on where and how you train it.

Regieleki and Regidrago are two of the golem Pokémon created by the legendary Regigigas. Both were once worshiped by humans, but the cult that worshipped them eventually sought to contain and seal away the powerful creatures instead.

Glastrier and Spectrier are two proud and rather cruel horse-like Pokémon that, were it not for Calyrex, would still be terrorizing the Galar region. Despite presenting them as quite menacing, Pokédexes everywhere are keen to point out that the horses also love a good snack.

Lastly there's Enamorus, who might sound like it's eligible to be in the 'largest Pokémon' club, but their name is instead tied to themes of renewed love - fitting for a supposed god of Springtime.

Gen 8 Mythical Pokémon

NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Zarude#893Dark/Grass600

Zarude was added to Pokémon Sword and Shield in the Isle of Armor DLC. It has a unique move, Jungle Healing, which restores health and removes status conditions for all your Pokemon in battle, making Zarude great for double battles.

Wo-Chien#1001Dark/Grass570

The core Pokémon Scarlet and Violet games added six new Legendary Pokemon Pokémon.

Wo-Chien, Chien-Pao, Ting-Lu, and Chi-Yu are known as the Calamity Pokémon. These badass Legendaries are actually cursed artifacts that absorded negative human emotions, came to life and formed bodies for themselves.

Koraidon, and Miraidon, meanwhile represent the past and future respectively. Dependent on game version, one of the two joins the player early on in Scarlet & Violet, becoming a Pokémon motorbike you can ride. We're not sure why they're needed in a world where both horse Pokémon and actual motor-vehicles exist, but they are very cool.

More Legendary Pokémon were added later in September 2023's Teal Mask DLC, forming the main storyline of that expansion's Kitakami region. These were Ogerpon - which can swap between four forms depending on the mask it's wearing - and its opposing numbers Okidogi, Munkidori, and Fezandipiti, the so-called Loyal Three.

Terapagos was added in the December 2023 Indigo Disk DLC. It's the  Legendary responsible for the 'Terastal phenomenon', which causes Pokémon to take on various new, jewel-like forms which alter their usual types.

Gen 9 Mythical Pokémon

NameImagePokédex #TypeBase Stat Total
Pecharunt#1025Poison/Ghost600

Pecharunt was added to Pokémon Scarlet and Violet in The Hidden Treasure of Area Zero Epilogue: Mochi Mayhem DLC, released in January 2024.

Unlike most Mythical Pokemon, which can easily be obtained via Mystery Gift, Pecharunt's event involved actual PLOT. You had to battle your way through trainers which Pecharunt had possessed with poisoned mochi, in order to eventually catch it.

Gen 10 Legendary Pokémon

Sorry trainers, the Legendary Pokémon of Generation 10 haven't been announced yet. You can find some rather dubious looking leaks and rumors online, but there's nothing concrete to show.

We can be sure that Pokémon Winds and Pokémon Waves will have legendary and mythical Pokémon though, presumably with one powerful beast representing the power of the skies and another embodying the seas. Perhaps it'll just be Kyogre and Rayquaza in false beards.

Fans are frankly unhealthily obsessed with this screenshot from the recent trailer. Is that suspiciously dark blob on the right the outline of a Legendary Pokémon? Or is it just a cloud? What if it's a cloud Pokémon?

Legendary Pokémon FAQ

What are Legendary Pokémon?

While there's no 'official' definition in Pokémon lore as to what exactly makes a Pokémon legendary, the general idea is that they're unique species (only one individual of each Legendary Pokémon exists) and are unusually powerful, although their power is often hidden, situational, or subtle in nature.

Legendaries often have some inherent, mystical connection to an aspect of the Pokémon world, in the manner of an animistic nature spirit, or the guardian deity of a human settlement or region.

In terms of game mechanics, they're usually non-evolving (single stage) Pokémon with unusually high in-game stats in one area or another, and they're usually genderless - although, as you read the rest of this section, you'll find that's not always true.

What seems to unite all Legendary Pokémon is that people in the Pokémon world tell stories about them, for one reason or another; they have a legend. Hence the name.

What's the difference between Legendary and Mythical Pokémon?

Legendary Pokémon are incredibly rare, but Mythical Pokémon are so rare that people in the Pokémon world doubt their very existence. In gameplay terms, there is one version of every Legendary Pokémon available in their respective games, but Mythical Pokémon were originally only obtainable during exclusive events. If you weren't around while they were being given away, there was no way to access them.

However, by now most Mythical Pokémon have either appeared in mainline games, or become accessible through other means, like completing a Pokédex on Pokémon HOME. Not all of them, though.  Zarude and Victini are the only two Mythicals that have never been released outside of limited-time events.

What is the strongest Legendary Pokémon?

All the Legendary Pokémon are pretty powerful, but in terms of pure raw stats, Arceus is the strongest. With 120 in every single statistic, Arceus has a base stat total of 720.

That said, other Legendary Pokémon have various forms that can match or even surpass the god of the Pokémon universe. Zacian and Zamazenta can match it in their Crowned Sword and Crowned Shield forms, for instance, and Terapagos comes close, with 700 stats in its Stellar Form.

But Mega Rayquaza and both forms of Mega Mewtwo are even stronger than Arceus, with combined stats totalling 780.

These are the most powerful Legendary Pokémon that a player can harness in-game, but even they are dwarfed by Eternamax Eternatus, which has a ridiculous stat total of 1,125. This is purely a boss fight however; the player cannot harness this legendary power themselves.

What's the weakest Legendary Pokémon?

Fans generally agree that Cosmog is the weakest Legendary Pokémon in the videogames. Its basic stats are pitiful and it can only learn two moves: Teleport (which switches it out of the battle) and Splash (which explicitly doesn't do anything).

Like Magikarp, its raison d'être is purely to evolve into stronger forms. In Cosmog's case, that's Cosmoem, followed by one of the twin Gen 7 Legendaries, Solgaleo and Lunala.

In the Pokémon TCG, Cosmog has a little more going for it. Some Cosmog cards allow you to draw cards and prevent damage to it while it's on your Bench. Ultimately, though, it's still a pitiable weakling that's only there to evolve into more powerful 'Mons.

What's the rarest Legendary Pokémon?

In the world of Pokémon, all the Legendary Pokémon are equally rare: there's just one of each of them. The Mythical Pokémon aren't rarer, they're just much less widely known about, and generally sighted more rarely by people in the world of Pokémon.

In our world, the rarest Legendary Pokémon from the videogames is most likely Diancie. The last time you could get a Diancie was at a 2016 South Korean real-world event, as a gift for Omega Ruby or Alpha Sapphire.

If we're talking Pokémon TCG, the rarest Legendary card, by value, is First Edition Neo Genesis Holo Lugia, from the year 2000. Experts reckon there are only 41 copies in the world that are graded at the PSA 10 'pristine' level - and one sold at auction in 2021 for a terrifying $114,300.

Who was the first Legendary Pokémon to exist?

The first Legendary Pokémon to exist in the Pokémon world was either Arceus or Mew - but there's no way to be sure which, and fan theories abound on either side.

Arceus, the 'god' of Pokémon, is said via in-game descriptions to have created the universe and every Pokémon in it; but Poké-scientists also believe Mew to be the 'ancestor' of all the other species.

Some fans theorize that they created each other in the time before time existed in the Pokémon universe - i.e. before Arceus created Dialga, the godlike Legendary Pokémon with power over time. But ultimately which came first - Arceus or Mew - will likely always remain a mystery.

Can Legendary Pokémon evolve?

Yes, some Legendary Pokémon can evolve - but most can't, and the ones that can sometimes do it in unusual ways, compared to regular Pokémon.

Gen 6's Type: Null (evolving into Silvally) and Cosmog (evolving into Cosmoem) were the first to have regular evolutions, with Cosmoem going on to evolve into either Solgaleo, in Pokémon Sun, or Lunala in Pokémon Moon.

There are several Mythical and Legendary Pokémon that have Mega Evolutions: Rayquaza, Mewtwo (which has an X and Y form), Latias, Latios, and Diancie.

Kyogre and Groudon also have 'Primal Reversions' introduce in Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire. They work a lot like Mega Evolutions, but are specific to those Pokémon.

Are there Legendary Pokémon cards?

Yes, Legendary Pokémon from every generation appear in a whole variety of cards for the Pokémon Trading Card Game. The more popular Legendary or Mythical 'mons often get picked for the fancier foil and illustration card treatments saved for the rarest printed cards, meaning they can end up being the most desirable to collect.

However, it's important to remember that that's not a rule in the TCG. Legendary and Mythical Pokémon have appeared on cards of all rarities, including standard common cards.

What are Pokémon LEGEND cards?

Briefly, during the HeartGold & SoulSilver card sets of the early 2010s, the Pokémon TCG introduced a small set of variant cards which exclusively featured Legendary Pokémon - their most distinctive aspect being that each 'card' was in fact two regular sized cards, which created a combined artwork when laid edge to edge.

Of the nine such two-card combos released, seven featured a pair of Legendaries together (one on each half). The other two are the two Gen 2 Legendary birds Ho-Oh and Lugia.

Wargamer regularly tracks down deals on Pokémon packs, and you can stay informed by joining our friendly Discord community.
