title: Top 50+ most expensive rare Pokémon cards of all time
content:
What are the most expensive Pokemon cards in the world? After 30 years of regular Pokémon TCG releases, there are quite a few staggeringly valuable cards out there. YouTuber Logan Paul famously blew over $5 million on a Pikachu Illustrator in 2022 and sold it in 2026 for $16 million, but that's just the tip of the iceberg.

We've searched online auction houses and scoured Pokémon history to find the 69 most valuable rare Pokémon cards ever sold (nice).

Because you're a true connoisseur, we know you'll want to read on for all those tasty, big money cards. But if you'd rather skip to the cream of the crop, hop straight to the top 10 most expensive Pokémon cards.

For details on how we track card sales for this guide, and expert tips on finding your own cards' value, you can also head to the FAQ section at the end of this guide.

These are the most expensive Pokémon cards:

69. Pokémon Card Fan Club Shining Magikarp

Price$14,000
Sale dateMay 24, 2023
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderBeckett
RatingGEM MT 9.5

Back in the early 90s, the Japanese Pokémon Card Fan Club (later succeeded by Pokémon Trainer's Card Magazine) advertised an extra-shiny Shining Magikarp promo. This fancy fish could only be won by obtaining 600 'GET points' at tournaments between 2000 and 2002.

As you can imagine, copies are fairly scarce. With so few available, it makes sense that a 9.5 gem mint copy fetched $14,000 on the auction site Fanatics Collect in 2023.

Functionally, the card is identical to Shining Magikarp from the regular 2002 Neo Genesis set. It has extremely similar art as well - you wouldn't know you had a gem at first glance.

What marks this Magikarp out from its school is the foiling. In the regular version, the background fish are shiny, whereas in the promo edition, it's the main, foreground Magikarp who shimmers. Just goes to show: when collecting rare Pokémon cards, the details matter.

68. Squirtle #29 Reverse Holo (Boundaries Crossed)

Price$15,000
Sale dateMarch 16, 2026
Auction houseEbay
GraderPSA
RatingPSA 10

Not all rare Pokémon cards start off rare. In fact, these days, it's not uncommon to see a pretty unremarkable card sell for silly money, merely because only a few people had the foresight to preserve a copy. 10+ years later, collectors will pay above the odds for one of the only top graded copies of that card in existence.

So it is with Squirtle #29 Reverse Holo from the 2012 set Boundaries Crossed. In late 2023, PriceCharting logged the sale of a PSA10 copy for just $250. But in March 2026, one sold for a princely $15,000 on Ebay, via the PSA Vault consignment service. That's a 5,900% increase in just over two years.

Reportedly, only two confirmed PSA 10 copies of the card exist, and the firms says it's only graded 37 copies at any grade - suggesting a vanishingly small pool of collectible-quality Squirtles out there. So it's certainly rare; only time will tell if paying 15 grand for this bathing cutie was a good investment.

67. First Edition Shining Charizard

Price$15,000
Sale dateOctober 30, 2022
Auction houseGoldin
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

One of the coolest Charizard cards ever printed, Shining Charizard from 2000's Neo Destiny set features a black shiny 'zard, with a foil treatment making the Pokémon literally 'shine'. Shining Pokemon were introduced in the previous set, Neo Revelation, and were very hard to get hold of, found in one pack in every 300 on average.

That scarcity was also reflected in the game's rules too. You were limited to only having one of each Shining card in your deck.

While still a darn sight less rare than their video game equivalents, Shining Pokémon in Neo Genesis were not common, so first edition versions that have remained in mint condition are now extremely scarce. The most expensive example of the card we found was this version, sold on eBay in January 1, 2025. It was originally listed for $17,999, but tracking sites like 130point claim the final selling price was $15,000.

66. Base Set First Edition Holo Mewtwo

Price$15,000
Sale dateApril 16 2023
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

For a certain generation of Pokémon fans, Mewtwo is the rare Pokémon, the rightful recipient of their Master Ball for (I probably threw mine at the first elemental bird I came across). It's unsurprising, then, that a card featuring the character would be worth something. Even more unsurprising is the fact it's the Base Set Shadowless 1st Edition Holo Mewtwo.

This card has everything - nostalgia, rarity, and a holographic background. It's also a shadowless card, meaning it was part of the first print run of the first English language Pokémon set. The most expensive copy we've seen sell is this PSA 10 copy sold via a Fanatics Collect auction in 2023.

65. Mega Charizard Y Poncho-wearing Pikachu

A rare Pokemon card depicting Pikachu wearing a cute little Poncho

Price$16,500
Sale dateSeptember 3 2026
Auction houseHeritage Auctions
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

Mega Charizard Y Poncho-wearing Pikachu was one of two promo cards in a special box set released only in Japan on January 1. The contents were pretty similar to those of an elite trainer box, except of course for this utterly adorable Pikachu, dressed up like the then new Mega Charizard Y.

64. Espeon Gold Star

Price$22,100
Sale dateFebruary 2021
Auction houseeBay
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

Get used to seeing the phrase 'gold star' when it comes to rare Pokémon cards. Essentially an evolution of the Shining Pokémon concept, gold star cards likewise show the alternate color 'shiny' variant of the Pokémon they depict - which is why this Espeon is green.

Few gold star Pokémon cards are ever printed - on average you'd find one in every two booster boxes, or 1/72 packs. This, and the fact they often feature gorgeous art of fan-favorite Pokémon, makes them extremely coveted.

Espeon Gold Star is a stunning example of this. Released in the promotional POP Series 5 set of 2007, this card regularly sells for thousands of dollars. A 2021 auction on eBay set the record high price of $22,100 for a PSA 10 copy.

Still, it's not the most valuable Eeveelution of that set - you'll learn more about that soon.

63. Gengar VMAX

Price$23,400
Sale dateAugust 2026
Auction houseeBay
GraderBGS
RatingBlack Label 10

The alt art version of Gengar VMAX from 2021's Fusion Strike was one of the set's most sought-after chases - unsurprising given the charismatic art for the popular Pokémon - but it's the Japanese version printed in the earlier High Class Deck that's achieved higher prices. As reported on social media by TCG Collectr, in August 2026 a BGS Black Label 10 copy of the Japanese card sold for $23,400 on eBay. The grading made a huge difference to the price, since a (comparatively lowly) PSA 10 that sold around the same time went for a "mere" $2,600.

62. HG&SS Undaunted Umbreon

Price$25,000
Sale dateMay 04, 2026
Auction houseeBay
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

Amidst all the special variants, errors cards, and promos you'll see on this list, it's kind of refreshing to have this entry, which is just a card featuring a Pokémon that people really like. Umbreon has almost as many diehard fans as Charizard. It's got a badass but cute design, it released in Gen 2 so there's plenty of nostalgia there, and it's an Eeveelution to boot.

In the modern era of the Pokémon TCG, we're pretty used to Umbreon SIRs being among a set's biggest chase cards, but it's even more true for older, rarer cards. This Umbreon, hailing from 2010's Undaunted set, sold in 2026 for $25,000 via eBay.

61. Japanese Basic No Rarity Symbol Holo Poliwrath

Price$25,015
Sale date2020
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

The 1996 Japanese Basic No Rarity Symbol Holo Poliwrath appeared in the original Pokémon base set, released in Japan in. Poliwrath isn't as widely popular as Charizard or Pikachu. Not quite the cutest Pokémon or the coolest, it's a bit of a sleeper in the original Pokédex. But every Pokémon is somebody's favorite.

At any rate, no collector in their right mind would turn down a PSA 10 card from the OG glory days of the Pokémon TCG. Proving our point, a 2020 auction from Fanatics Collect saw the water Pokémon sell for $25,015.

We should mention that the missing rarity symbol isn't a printing error, but a sign of authenticity. The first printings of first edition Pokémon cards in Japan lacked the symbol in the bottom corner. Japan didn't have shadowless cards, but these are essentially the equivalent.

60. 2009 Japanese Design Promo Spikey Eared Pichu

Price$25,800
Sale dateJune 2023
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

In 2009, as a promotion for the movie 'Arceus and the Jewel of Life', the Japanese publishing company Shogakukan held a drawing contest for children and young teens. Contestants were asked to share artwork for Arceus or Spikey-Eared Pichu, with the winners being turned into actual Pokémon cards. This delightful floral Pichu was designed by the second-grade winner, who was around seven or eight years old at the time.

According to Dicebreaker, only 13 to 100 copies of this card are thought to exist, and only three copies of Spikey-Eared Pichu have ever been graded by PSA. It's no wonder, then, that the 2009 Japanese Design Promo 2nd Grade Winner Spikey-Eared Pichu card can fetch such a high price, with a Fanatics Collect auction reaching $25,800 in June 2023.

59. Gold Pikachu

Price$29,520
Sale dateSeptember 2021
Auction houseGoldin
RatingEX 5

Nothing screams expensive like a flash of gold. And in this case, gold beats old. The Gold Pikachu Pokémon card was released in 2018, to mark the 20th anniversary of the Pokémon TCG.

Made of 11 grams of solid 24-karat gold, the card is a replica of the original Japanese Pikachu card's design, featuring a very round yellow mouse. To grab the card on release, buyers first entered a lottery, with winners given the chance to buy the limited edition card for a cool ¥216,000 ($2,000 / £1,700).

Since then, its value has risen swiftly. It sold for close to $8,000 (£5,750) in 2019, then $12,655 in 2020. Most recently, a version of the card went for a cool $29,520 in 2021. Notably, this was graded at EX 5 by PSA, so higher-priced Pikachu's are certainly possible

Although not legal in tournament play, the card came with a handy glass frame to display the artifact to visitors. You'd probably have to explain why spending nearly 30 grand on a single, unusable card was a good financial decision, though.

58. Darkrai #BW73

Price$30,000
Sale dateApril 27, 2026
Auction houseEbay
GraderPSA
Rating10

These days, nothing seems to send a Pokémon card's price rocketing quite like its featured 'Mon becoming the mascot of a brand new expansion. Consequently, the reveal of new Japanese set Abyss Eye, in April 2026, sent high-rolling collectors scrambling for high graded copies of older Darkrai cards.

Top of the pile is the remarkably imposing-looking 2013 Black & White promo card Darkrai #BW73, which sold in PSA 10 for a record price of $30,000 on Ebay, in the same month Abyss Eye was unveiled.

That's a staggering markup from the previous PSA 10 sale we found just two months before - a comparatively casual $15k - and more than three times the one before that, which fetched only $8,700 in late 2025. This, for a card from 2013's Team Plasma box, which at the time retailed for 20 bucks.

57. X/Y 20th Anniversary Festa Pikachu

Price$32,250
Sale dateSeptember 3 2023
Auction houseGoldin
GraderBeckett
RatingPristine 10

While the Japanese X/Y 20th Anniversary Festa Pikachu is pretty recent as far as rare Pokémon cards go, it has a classic feel that older fans will still adore. It helps that all three Gen 1 starter Pokémon - plus the biggest icon of the IP, Pikachu - feature in its vibrant, adorable artwork.

This pricey piece of paper was given out to attendees of the 2016 Anniversary Festa in Toki Messe, Niigata, which took place to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the first-ever Pokémon game.

Its abilities aren't likely to win you tournaments, but they are pretty unique. A 120-damage attack 'Mega Thunderbolt' causes you to discard all Pikachu's energy, and the Celebration ability demands that every player clap their hands and then draw a card.

The highest-selling copy of this card was sold on March 9, 2023 via auction site Goldin. This card, given Beckett's maximum grade of 10 (Pristine) fetched $32,520 at auction.

56. Shining Mew CoroCoro Promo

Price$33,000
Sale dateJanuary 17, 2025
Auction houseeBay
GraderARS
Rating10

Featuring a lovely, baby blue Shiny Mew, this Japanese Shining Mew CoroCoro promo card is incredibly hard to get hold of. It's one of Japan's unnumbered promo cards, which have short print runs attached to specific events like tournaments and film releases.

In this case, Shining Mew was a promo card released in the May 2001 issue of a magazine, the kids manga CoroCoro. As you might expect for a freebie given out in a children's comic, few copies survived in good nick. Which is why a version of this Japanese card sold in January 2025 for a whopping $33,000.

55. 2002 Trophy Card Neo Summer Battle Road No. 2 Trainer

Price$34,100
Sale dateMarch 2021
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderBeckett
Rating7.5 NRMT

The 2002 Trophy Card Neo Summer Battle Road No. 2 Trainer is a card with a real mouthful of a name. Its value more than makes up for this, as this is a card whose value is as high as its name is long.

The 2002 TCNSBRN2T (as we won't be calling it) was the second-place prize in the Junior Division of 2002's Kanto Summer Battle Road tournament. The recipient of this promo was Fukinishi Tomoki - a fact we know because their name and the region they competed in are included on the card.

Prize promo cards, especially those with a unique name printed on them, are extremely hard to come by. For example, the priciest copy of this card was sold via Fanatics Collect in March 2021 for a cool $34,100, despite having a middling grade of 7.5 Near Mint.

54. Topps Chrome Charizard Tekno #06

Price$35,000
Sale dateAugust 27 2023
Auction houseeBay
GraderPSA
Rating10

Back in the 2000s, collectibles manufacturer Topps held the coveted Pokémon TCG production license. Among the early cards it produced was Topps Chrome Charizard Tekno #06, a particularly rare and particularly shiny card featuring one of the game's most popular 'mons.

Topps produced three types of shiny Pokémon cards, and of the three, Tekno-Chrome cards had the rarest pull rates. This means this Charizard was hard to hunt down at the time it was printed - nowadays, copies of this vintage card are even more scarce.

The highest sale price on record for a Tekno Topps Charizard can be found on Price Charting, which records an eBay sale from August 2023 of $35,000. The pristine quality of this card, which was graded a 10 by PSA, has clearly helped push up the price.

53. First Edition Holo Crystal Charizard

Price$40,800
Sale dateOctober 16 2022
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

While it's not the most popular card featuring this iconic Pokémon, the Holographic Crystal Charizard is pretty unique. It's an e-card that, when scanned with an e-reader, reveals bonus content like mini-games or Pokédex info.

This was a novelty that didn't stick around long. Mysterious Mountains (the set that Holo Crystal Charizard hails from) was the last Japanese expansion to include e-cards. It, along with its English-language equivalent Skyride, was also the last set produced by Wizards of the Coast before the publisher's Pokémon license ran out.

All this makes the card a rare and interesting part of Pokémon history. Combine that with the fact it's a Charizard Pokémon card, and you've got a recipe for high value. So far, the most we've seen Crystal Charizard sell for is $40,800 (£32,300) in an auction from October 2022.

52. Holo Gold Star Torchic

Price$43,200
Sale dateOctober 2021
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
RatingGEM MT 10

Printed gold star cards are hard to come by, and well-preserved copies are even rarer. That's what makes the Holographic Gold Star Torchic so expensive - PSA has so far recorded that only 19 copies with the pristine GEM MT 10 grade exist. It was one such gem that sold in April 2022 for $43,200 (£34,200).

Gold star cards are popular for their rarity, but their gorgeous art is also part of the appeal. Masakazu Fukuda's adorable rendition of Torchic, popping out of the frame with a cheeky wink and a flash of glitter, is sure to drive up the sentimental and fiscal value of the card.

51. Pikachu MTG Stock Test Proof

Price$45,000
Sale dateJune 2025
Auction houseHeritage Auctions
RatingPSA Authentic

It turns out that one of the most expensive Pokémon cards ever sold was actually a Magic: The Gathering card. Pikachu MTG Stock Test Proof is evidence that Wizards of the Coast did some printer testing before releasing its Base Set.

Here, we can see the adorable, chubby Pikachu from said set, printed on the back of an entirely unrelated TCG card. That happens to be Independent Troops from the Magic: The Gathering set Portal Three Kingdoms. Despite being printed on the back, Pikachu remains legible, vibrant, and as cute as ever.

This is certainly one of the more unique Pokémon cards, as it represents a bit of the game's history. It's also the only authenticated copy of the card to exist. That, no doubt, is why it sold for almost $50,000 at auction.

50. 2000 Tropical Mega Battle No. 1 Trainer

Price$48,125
Sale dateSeptember 2023
Auction houseHeritage Auctions
GraderCGC
RatingPristine 10

These promo cards were awarded to first-place winners of Japan's regional tournaments in 2000, which also saw the victors qualify for that year's Tropical Mega Battle tournament. Two versions of this promo card actually exist, depicting a male or a female trainer, and they were reportedly awarded to contestants based on their gender.

A precursor to more established competitive Pokémon competitions, Tropical Mega Battle took place annually in Hawaii between 1999 and 2001, and was the first major international competition for young Pokémon TCG fans. The competition included American and Japanese children (more countries were added after the first year) but only Japanese kids got these trophy cards.

Heritage Auctions claims that this copy of 2000 No. 1 Trainer Tropical Mega Battle is the only one to receive a Pristine 10 rating from CGC. However, despite its excellent condition, other, rarer trainer promos have sold for far higher prices.

49. Holo Gold Star Rayquaza

Price$48,958
Sale dateJune 1 2023
Auction houseCOLLECTR
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

EX Deoxys is one of the rarest Pokémon packs of all time, and Holographic Gold Star Rayquaza is its biggest chase card. Like all the rare gold star cards, this features a shiny Pokémon, and the card has a holographic sparkle. But few gold star Pokémon cards are as coveted as the stylish black and gold shiny Rayquaza.

This rare card from 2005 sold for a whopping $45,100 (£35,867) in 2020. We thought it may have peaked in value - as much more recently, a PSA 10 copy of the card went for just $38,100 (£30,300) - but apparently not, as on June 1, 2023, Rayquaza sold again for $48,598.

48. Master Scroll

Price$50,000
Sale dateAugust 2020
Auction houseeBay
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

The 2010 Master Scroll Trophy Card was an award given to the most dedicated members of the Japanese Pokémon fan club, the Daisuki Club.

The Daisuki Club was responsible for distributing promo cards to players between 2007 - 2010, after the Player's Club shut down. Fans could earn 'Action Points' through various activities, quizzes, and competing in tournaments, and the Master Scroll promo was the grand prize, given only to those who earned 8,600 points.

A grade 9 Master Scroll sold on eBay for somewhere in the ballpark of $50,000 (£40,000) (though it was an accepted offer, so we can't be sure of an exact price).

While the Daisuki Club still persists to this day, it no longer gives out unique promos.

47. 1999 Tropical Mega Battle No. 2 Trainer

Price$50,300
Sale date2020
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingAuthentic

The Tropical Mega Battle No. 2Trainer prize card was issued to the second place prize winner in 1999's Mega Battle Tournament, a seven-tournament grand slam culminating in a finals in Hawaii. The prize cards, which auctioneer Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC) states were given to the top three players from each region, all featured Exeggutor - a reference to the tournament's location.

Hardly any copies of this card have ever been professionally graded, so their rare auction appearances command a high price, regardless of how well preserved they are.

46. Wonder Platinum Japan National Championship Promo

Price$51,250
Sale dateDecember 2023
Auction houseHeritage Auctions
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

The Wonder Platinum Japan National Championship Promo was given to competitors in the 2009 Japan World Championship representative Pokémon tournament. Winners of this national tournament would then be put forward for the 2009 World Championships. Only 20 copies were ever handed out, meaning this is an incredibly rare prize card.

While there's no adorable or epic Pokémon in its artwork, Wonder Platinum still features some quality illustration. Plus, the name is a reference to 2008's Pokémon Platinum.

45. Mega Charizard X ex Black Label

Price$54,100
Sale dateMarch 2026
Auction houseEbay
GraderBeckett
RatingBGS 10 Black Label

Pokémon card grading - paying a company money to measure every micron of your card and officially rate how perfect it is out of ten - is now crucial to the value of high-end cards. Half a point up or down on your grading can make thousands, tens of thousands, or in a few cases over a million dollars' worth of difference to the price.

Arguably the most extreme and exacting (and therefore desirable) grading for a card to get is Beckett's coveted 'Black Label' - which requires a perfect 10 on all four of the company's key metrics: surface, edges, corners, and centering.

Achieving that almost impossible, unicorn quality standard is what, in March 2026, transformed a copy of Phantasmal Flames' Mega Charizard X ex from an $800 card (very respectable, for a modern chase that only came out four months prior) to one that sold for over $54,000, winning it a seat in this all-time hall of fame.

44. Base Set First Edition Holo Chansey

Price$55,000
Sale date2020
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

The 1999 Base Set 1st Edition Shadowless Holo Chansey is an original Pokémon card depicting a unique and popular Pokémon. It may be no Charizard, but Chansey has plenty of fans nonetheless and - perhaps surprisingly - is one of the most expensive Base Set cards, at least in good condition.

A PSA 10 Chansey card is very hard to come by. It's that holographic finish on the card - it scratches very easily. The lighter background makes those scratches show up more clearly and so, of the 16 holo cards from Base set, Chansey is by far the hardest to find in PSA 10 condition.

It's also theorized that early Pokémon players may have been prejudiced against the pink, nurturing Chansey Pokémon, and may have taken less good care of the card than they did with favorites like Charizard or Venusaur.

The highest sale of such a card for quite some time was $36,877 in October 2020, but then in July 2024 it was topped with an eye-watering $55,000 sale!

43. Base Set No Rarity Venusaur

Price$55,000
Sale date2021
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

First edition Pokémon cards are already a winner. And while Venusaur doesn't have the same pull as Charizard, this starter evolution still does stonks on the secondary market.

Base Set No Rarity Venusaur is made even more valuable because of a printing problem - the black star in the bottom right that's meant to denote the card's rarity, is missing. Oh, and this one in particular has the protective case signed by artist Mitsuhiro Arita. All in all, that led to a price of $55,000 (£43,700) at a PWCC auction in 2021 - though since the auctioneer has rebranded as Fanatics Collect the listing has gone from the site.

42. 64 Mario Stadium Snap Articuno

Price$58,560
Sale dateJuly 2024
Auction houseGoldin
GraderPSA
RatingCGC Pristine 10

One of a number of entries on this list from the Pokémon Snap contest run in 1999, this card was made thanks to a competition run by the Nintendo-focused Japanese TV show 64 Mario Stadium. Participants were asked to send in their greatest Pokémon snapshots from the game, and the best five were made into real Pokémon cards. The manga magazine CoroCoro Comic ran the same competition - also creating five cards.

Like all the Pokémon Snap cards, 20 copies of the 64 Mario Stadium Snap Articuno card were made. Functionally, it's identical to the version released in the Pokémon TCG set Fossil, though obviously with unique art. Only six copies have been logged by PSA according to Goldin, where this near mint copy sold for $58,560.

41. Tropical Mega Battle Bilingual Exeggutor

Price$59,780
Sale dateApril 2024
Auction houseGoldin
GraderCGC
RatingPSA NM/MT 8

This unusual Exeggutor card with text in both Japanese and English was given out to all 50-odd participants of the 1999 Tropical Mega Battle finals, which took place in Hawaii. Like some of the other prize cards awarded at that tournament, it features the palm tree Pokémon Exeggutor, see here enjoying island living.

The most expensive sale we could find for the Tropical Mega Battle Bilingual Exeggutor card was on the auction site Goldin in April 2024, where it went for 59,780. The rarest and most collectable Pokémon cards are generally those cards with extremely limited print runs - and often low quality copies of these can still go for thousands. In this case though, both the rarity and the quality was high, as the card had a Pristine 10 from grading company CGG.

40. 2005 Summer Battle Road Mew Victory Orb

Price$60,000
Sale date28 December 2020
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

The 2005 Summer Battle Road Mew Victory Orb was a prize given out at the 2005 Summer Battle Road tournament. There were nine regional competitions as part of this tournament, and the top three players in each would receive this Mew Victory Orb card. This means only a handful of copies were ever given out.

This particular copy of the card, sold in 2020, received a PSA grading of 10, and it was auctioned with its original trophy case. This helped it fetch a tidy price of $60,000 (£47,500).

39. Ex Dragon Frontiers Holo Gold Star Charizard

Price$60,066
Sale dateOctober 2020
Auction houseeBay
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

The Ex Dragon Frontiers Holo Charizard Gold Star was a rare Pokémon card, even when it was first printed in 2006. It's one of several 'gold star' cards in this guide, which have a pull rate of one every two booster boxes. Combine this with a PSA 10 grading and the most popular Pokémon to ever grace the game, and its no surprise that one reached $66,000 in an eBay auction in October 2020.

This might not be the most recognizable, powerful, or expensive of the Charizards out there, but it does have some of the most unique art. Masakazu Fukuda presents a dark version of the darling dragon, leaping through the air while letting out bursts of flame.

While they're all but forgotten these days, "Ex" cards were the big hotness in the scene during the early-to-mid aughts, and many are worth big cash now - read our full guide to Pokémon Ex cards for more info.

38. 64 Mario Stadium Chansey

Price$63,000
Sale dateDecember 2022
Auction houseFanatics Collect (formerly PWCC)
GraderBeckett
RatingNM / MT 8.5

While promoting the 1999 Nintendo 64 game Pokémon Snap, Nintendo held two fan contests where pictures taken in the videogame would be turned into real Pokémon cards. Ten winners were selected from each; winners of the CoroCoro Comic contest received 20 copies of their personalized card, while winners of the 64 Mario Stadium contest got just 15. As you can imagine, a 64 Mario Stadium Chansey (with art by competition winner Kaori Someya) is pretty rare.

Making them even rarer still is the fact that, according to Fanatics Collect, only two copies of the card have ever been sold. One auctioned for $63,000 ($50,000) back in December 2022, which shows just how much one of these Pokémon Snap cards could be worth if they ever appear again.

37. 2013 World Championships Pikachu No. 1 Trainer

Price$63,000
Sale dateDecember 2 2022
Auction houseHeritage Auctions
GraderPSA
RatingMT 9

It does get a little older, however, as these Presentation cards are actually the third version of early Pokémon cards. They're not to be confused with the earlier black and white prototype cards, which featured Gameboy sprites, or the beta playtest cards used to try out the rules. We've got a separate article that explains the full history, and how it came to light. Here's the short version. In 1999 when WotC was getting ready to make the prerelease Clefable card, the initial version of the print sheet contained a small number of base set Raichus as well as the Clefables. The error was caught during production proofing and corrected, so only a tiny number of the Raichus were ever made, either eight or eleven according to different versions of the story.

All the copies of the card went home with Wizards of the Coast employees, who held onto them and occasionally teased fans by showing them off at public events. It wasn't until 2006 that they were confirmed to exist, and not until 2023 until any of the cards were graded. And so far as we know, a 2025 sale of one of the cards for $550,000 is the only time they've ever changed hands!

Maybe the buyer liked the adorably tiny trophy; maybe the bronze sparkly finish simply looks a bit more like the gold of the No. 1 trophy card below.

Or maybe, in between 2023 and 2026, Pokémon cards have begun attracting so much more attention from the ultra-wealthy that the very rarest specimens are now a fashionable status symbol for billionaires (or those who wish to appear to be billionaires) to flaunt at each other.

Maybe the top end of this is mostly an ego playground for fabulously rich men who'll happily spend $1.77m - the cost of 4.1 million meals for starving people, according to the World Food Programme - on a 2.5 by 3.5 inch rectangle of cardboard, just because they can. Does it bring them as much joy as it brought a Japanese teenager at the end of one triumphant weekend in the late 90s? We can only imagine.

3. Trophy Pikachu No. 1 Trainer

Price$3,000,000
Sale dateSeptember 12, 2025
Auction houseeBay
GraderPSA
RatingMINT 9

Sitting right at the top of the Trophy Pikachu Tree, fittingly, is 1998's Trophy Pikachu No.1 Trainer - extremely limited promos handed only to the winning Pokémon players at the TCG's second-ever sanctioned tournament, the 1997-98 Japanese Lizardon Mega Battle Pokémon competition.

Just like its promo prize siblings, the number-one Pikachu was illustrated by Mitsuhiro Arita. This time, the world's most popular Pokémon is lifting a trophy in the air, grinning in triumph.

Supposedly, there are only 14 copies of this card, period. We've seen others sell for thousands upon thousands, but none have quite matched the price of the copy sold in September 2025. It's understandable - MINT 9 might be the best grading we've ever seen this promo get. No.1 Trainer Pikachu is a true winner, indeed.

2. Raincoat Pikachu - perhaps

Price$8,400,000
Sale dateSeptember 28, 2026
Auction houseFanatics Collect
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

Raincoat Pikachu was created as a prize for a competition tied to the 3DS game Pokémon Art Academy in 2015; fans had to draw Pikachu in the game and upload it to the Miiverse social network. Six winners each got 100 copies of the promotional Pikachu card featuring their very own illustration.

This is a rare card to be sure, and in September 2026 a copy sold for a massive $8,400,000 (including buyer's premium) on Fanatics Collect - at least, it seems like it did. There's actually some doubt.

Reporters at Chase Society noticed that this auction listing was removed from Fanatics Collect entirely, which is usually a sign that the buyer has failed to pay. The listing then returned to the site. As of November 13 2026 it's still up, but scrutinizing the page source data shows that it has the "cancelled" status. There's an error in the data, it's just not clear where, so we're keeping an eye on this one.

1. Pikachu Illustrator

Price$16,492,000
Sale dateFebruary 16, 2026
Auction houseGoldin
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

The new holy grail of the TCG, Pikachu Illustrator is a promo Pokémon card originally handed out to winners of a 1998 illustration competition run through Japanese magazine CoroCoro. Only 39 copies were ever created.

It's the only card to feature the 'Illustrator' title instead of 'Trainer'. The artwork was drawn by esteemed Pokémon illustrator Atsuko Nishida, creator of Pokémon's main mascot, Pikachu. There's even a unique pen icon in the bottom-right corner, seen on no other card.

It's unknown exactly how many Pikachu Illustrator cards are still in existence, but ten PSA certified copies have been graded as 'mint'. From January 2021 onwards, it was the most expensive Pokémon card to ever be sold at auction, with a PSA 9 Mint condition card selling for a whopping $233,000 (£167,600).

Though it lost the title briefly, in July 2021 Logan Paul (yeah, that guy) spent $4 million on the only existing PSA 10 version of the card, getting the purchase accredited by Guinness World Records as the most expensive Pokémon card ever sold. But the value of the card was actually even higher: to secure the trade, Paul also handed over a lesser PSA 9 version of the card, which he'd previously purchased for $1,275,000.

The saga of this card doesn't end there. In early 2026, Mr Paul went on to sell the card to one AJ Scaramucci, once again getting Guinness involved. That's because the sales figure this time was a frankly staggering $16,492,000.

We should add that Logan also parted ways with the diamond-encrusted necklace he'd been carrying the card around in (does a $1 card taped to a $2 million car cost $2,000,001?) But even so, it's more than fair to call this the most expensive Pokémon card of all time!

It's a pity it's so rare: Pikachu looks even cuter than usual holding an oversized fountain pen.

Bonus - Black Triangle Base Set Booster Pack

Price$2,700
Sale dateUnverified
Auction houseeBay
RatingN/A

We're including a bonus curiosity because it's just too interesting not to mention. When Wizards of the Coast realized they had accidentally printed too many Base Set booster packs branded with the first-edition logo, they covered the errant symbol with a small black triangle. A simple attempt to avoid wasting resources has generated a much-prized collector's item, as fans now clamor for a rare Black Triangle Base Set Booster Pack.

It's the packaging itself that's valuable here, not the cards inside, so don't go cracking one of these black triangle packs open if you happen to find one sitting in the back of a drawer (you lucky devil).

They're occasionally found in standard Base Set booster boxes - so if you have one you'll have to weigh up whether to gamble on the chance discovery of one of the black triangle booster packs, or whether it's best to leave the box unopened for its pristine value. Some of the black triangle boosters have fetched over $2,700 (£2,000) on eBay, depending upon their condition and which Pokémon is displayed on their cover.

Rare Pokémon cards FAQ

How we find the most expensive Pokémon cards

To compile this list, we come back each month to trawl the latest sales on global trading card and collectibles auction houses like Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC), Heritage Auctions, and Goldin Auctions. We aim to keep the rankings and prices as up to date as possible.

Remember that, like all collectibles and investments, the Pokémon card market is very volatile, and prices can change fast and often. If you're looking to buy and sell high value Pokémon cards, you need to take care to double check the latest prices, being very conscious of the website or auction house's commission rates and fees.

Which Pokémon cards are rarest?

The most valuable Pokémon cards normally command high prices because they're old and there are very few copies in circulation. Most originate from the earliest Pokémon sets, or are one-off tournament prize cards printed in very low numbers. First edition Pokémon cards, peculiar misprints, and desirable old promos all fetch very high prices.

How to tell if a Pokémon card is rare?

Wargamer has a dedicated guide to Pokémon card rarity covering the basic rarity levels of cards you can open in any pack. If you think an old card you've gotten hold of could be particularly valuable, our guides to first edition Pokémon cards and shadowless Pokémon cards will help you to identify them. It's also worth referring to our guide to fake Pokémon cards, as there are plenty of counterfeits on the market.

How to sell rare Pokémon cards

We have a dedicated guide on how to sell Pokémon cards, so we recommend you read that if you're considering trading - but here's the short version.

If you think you're holding a truly valuable Pokémon card, your first port of call is to get it protected by placing it in a thin, soft-plastic sleeve, then into a protective, hard-plastic 'toploader' case. Before spending any more money on the card, it's usually a good idea to show it to an expert in-person, to get their opinion on its condition and potential value. A specialist at your local games store may be able to help.

Then you should get it graded by a well-regarded, expert grading service - PSA Pokémon card grading is the most popular in the USA. Once you get the card back with an official grading from 1 to 10, and stored in a professional PSA protective case, you should have a good idea what price range you're likely to get for it.

Bear in mind that there's usually a huge difference in value between a PSA grade 7, 8, or 9 card (generally mint condition to the naked eye) and a perfect PSA 10 card (absolutely faultless, even when viewed under a microscope from every angle). The really high prices paid by top level collectors are only for PSA 10 cards, and a PSA 10 is very often worth more than twice as much as the exact same card at PSA grade 8 or 9.

If you don't find any ultra-valuable Pokémon cards in your collection, it's really not the end of the world. This is a game, remember - what you have got is a delightful collection to treasure and play with. If you want to share any new pack pulls or treasured classics with a community of fellow fans, you're most welcome in the Wargamer Discord!

To keep up to date with the latest news about new rare cards and any bargains we find, subscribe to the Wargamer newsletter.

title: Trench Crusade Warband Focus: High Cathedra of Pride
content:
Welcome to another Trench Crusade Warband Focus. This week we're focusing on the self-styled first among all the Sins, Pride.

The Lore

Pride is the first of all Sins, and as such it's seat, the High Cathedra of Pride, is given privilege over the other six Serpent Heads in the incomprehensibly intricate machinations of the Court. The most recent holder of the seat is Eligos, the Grand Duke of Petals. They have not made any overt moves in the war against Creation recently, but they took the largest loan from Mammon in the history of the war in order to finance the construction of the automaton legions that took Rejika in 1872. From this beachhead into European mainland no doubt they will continue to press forward when the time is right.

Unwilling to let any who they march against be unaware of the glory of whom they face, all of the legions of Pride march under resplendent banners that glow with an eerie and unbearable light as a blinding perversion of the Heavenly Hosts they mock.

Defining Traits of the High Cathedra of Pride

Pride does not have particularly harsh restrictions, especially compared to some of the other Sins like Envy. As per usual, you must take either a Praetor or a Sorcerer to lead the warband. In addition you MUST purchase a troop flag, which either an ELITE or Desecrated Saint must carry.

Court Praetor Credit: Darius Minis

While your flag-carrying model is not Down or Out of Action, your entire warband scores critical hits on an 11+ instead of on a 12. This may not sound huge at first, but this will drastically increase the number of critical hits you can expect to land throughout a game. You'll see this the most with high attack bonus models like the Praetor.

It is against the nature of Pride to retreat from any confrontation. As such, if any of your models take a retreat move your opponent may place one Blessing Marker next to any model in their warband. Yoke Fiends within the Court of Pride are simply not allowed to voluntarily retreat without wearing a restraining muzzle.

Sorcerer
Credit: Darius Minis

Pride has very fitting SIN generation. If any of your ELITE models activate in Open terrain without touching any terrain that could give them the benefit of Cover they gain 2 SIN markers. Your Praetor and Sorcerer also have an additional method, if they activate within 18 inches and line of sight of a Wretched (friend or foe) they gain 1 SIN from their inherent sense of superiority. This generally means you will keep an entourage of a few Wretched near your leader, especially with the unique wretched equipment available to Pride. Pride lacks any unique method of SIN generation for its basic troops, but the peons can still gain SIN from the Desecrated Saint which gives one SIN to any model that activates within one inch of them (including themselves) and the classic Torture Instrument. But really, if you are playing Pride then your game plan is most likely all about the Elites. You'll usually start the game with a glut of SIN from safe out of sight activations when Cover isn't needed, but leaving your Elites in the open for SIN generation in later turns is more of a risk that you need to consider as the game goes on.

Battlekit Highlights

All of the Seats get their own special little toys to play with, and Pride has an assortment truly befitting the First Sin.

The Cloak of the Morningstar is a fantastic suit of armor. It is INNATE, so there is no risk of losing it in a campaign to a particularly unlucky Trauma Roll. Aside from being a way of giving one of your ELITE models a -3 INJURY MODIFIER without taking up one of their valuable hands, and as such I like putting it on a Praetor with the Serpent Assault Gun and the Malebranche Sword. It also makes the model completely immune to being made to take a forced move. For three Glory this item is an absolute steal. It can also be given to a Desecrated Saint, if you really want to prevent them from being moved around by tricky opponents.

Glorious Light is a defensive item available to your Hellknights and Desecrated Saint. For a mere Twenty Ducats you inflict -1 DICE to the Success Roll for all attacks that target the model with the Light. Added to a Desecrated Saint with a Polearm this can make them surprisingly difficult to shift.

Desecrated Saint
Credit: Darius Minis

Laurels of the Supreme is extremely dependent on your terrain set up. If you have a board with a lot of vertical play space it can be a fantastic boon. If you play on a more flat set up, it is a Combat Helmet that costs Three Glory. If at any point in the activation of a model with the Laurels it can draw line of sight to an enemy model that is at least 2 inches below it, you can give yourself one Blessing Marker. Up to 6 Blessing Markers a game can be a massive swing in your favor, and you don't need to begin or end your activation in the open to gain it, so a DASH action combined with a Praetors 8 inch FLIGHT movement means it is easier than it might first seem to get multiple uses out of it. It is less of an immediate Glory purchase than the Cloak of the Morningstar, but still a strong item.

The Lightbringer Rifle is an expensive weapon at 40 Ducats, and aside from CRITICAL it lacks any obvious enhanced killing power for its high cost. But it's special abilities are where it shines. Think of this as a reverse Laurels of the Supreme. Where that item revels in being above others, the Lightbringer is the raw venomous spite at any who dare to raise themselves above you given lethal form. You add +3 DICE to any Ranged Attack targeting a model that it as least 2 inches above the wielder. In addition to that, if the attack is a success the target will automatically Fall if it is within 2 inches of any open window, unattended door or ominous ledge. While not always lethal, this is always hilarious.

Eligos's namesake, the Petals of the Blood Roses are given to the most deserving of Wretched to scatter at the feet of their masters. A strange bit of defensive utility against BLAST weapons, the Petals of the Blood Roses let you scatter incoming attacks by 1d6 inches if they have the BLAST Keyword and would hit a friendly DEMONIC model within 3 inches of the petal-bearing Wretched. You must have line of sight from the initial target point to wherever it ends up. For just 5 Ducats this is a cheap utility item for the Wretched that you likely will have following your Praetor and Sorcerer around anyway as you will want to get the benefit of Superiority.

The Power of Pride

Light of Samael

Everyone's favorite SIN powered unholy laser remains our number one spell. You pick an enemy in line of sight and within 24 inches, and you roll Injury for them. If they survive, and are on 40mm or smaller base, you knock them back 1d6 inches. The utility of an attack that automatically hits at 24 inches is not to be underestimated, and now this Goetic Power specifically states that they move even if they are Down. As if we needed more ways to knock people out of windows.

Proud Defiance

Have you ever forgotten that Trench Crusade has a Morale system? Well keep on forgetting it with this power that makes you immune to the entire thing! Honestly not a huge fan of this power, but it can be of some use as Pride tends to be a fairly tall building Sin focused on a smaller number of more powerful models and only a few losses could potentially trigger a Morale check.

Too Proud to Fall

The other Pride Classic, I am less sold on this one however. While not going Down for 2 SIN per instance of it can be useful for your long term survival, especially if your model is in melee, the BLOOD MARKERS from any attacks that would cause the Down result still stack up. It can be a life saver for an attack or two, but don't expect it to keep you alive if you leave a model completely exposed.

Wounded Pride

Our newest ability, if a model without ELITE would place BLOOD MARKERS on the model with this spell, you place the same number of BLOOD MARKERS on the attacking model. Not exactly a rubber and glue scenario, but very it is deliciously spiteful and very tasty on a Hellknight.

Playing the Warband

Pride lists lean tall. Get your ELITE core going strong, with at least two of the Big Three included in every list. Those being Praetor, Sorcerer and Hunter of the Left Hand Path. I then recommend getting a Saint and a few Yokes and Wretched to fill in as needed. But taking a Hellknight for a banner bearer is also an option if you can't afford a Saint and don't want to give it to the Hunter. Remember, you are required to take a Troop Banner.

Hunter of the Left Hand Path Credit: Darius Minis

If you can do so safely, you want to deploy in a group around your Desecrated Saint to maximize SIN generation for your first turn, as you will want a lot of it and likely won't be able to freely get as much in future rounds. Your primary SIN generation relies on your ELITE models starting their activation's not in COVER. This is less safe as the game goes on, but is possible if there is large line of sight blocking terrain to take advantage of. Otherwise you may need to nurse your initial harvest of SIN for several turns.

The Big Three will live up to their name in a Pride list. You will likely not have any significant killing power other than them for a majority of lists so you really need to make each of their activations count. I enjoy really using the multi-kill potential of the Praetor when you can position them well. Taking one or two softer targets out with the Serpent Assault Gun and then charging into a different threat with a Malebranche backed up by the Light of Samael to add an extra hit that can push the target out of melee and generate another swing with that deliciously deadly Malebranche means you can significantly thin out the opposing force if you position them well.

Sample List

800 Ducats, 6 Glory

Elites

Praetor - 224D | 3G

Upgrades & Choices: Too Proud to Fall, Light of Samael

Battlekit: Serpent Assault Gun, Malebranche Sword, Sword/Axe, Cloak of the Morning Star

Sorcerer - 138D

Upgrades & Choices: Light of Samael, Proud Defiance, Blessing of the Serpent Moon

Battlekit: Trench Club, Standard Armor, Trench Shield.

Hunter of the Left-Hand Path - 140D | 1G

Hunter of the Left-Hand Path – 140D | 1G

Battlekit: Bow of Lethe, Head Taker, Cthonic Vessel, Standard Armor

Troops

Desecrated Saint - 161D

Battlekit: Polearm, Sword/Axe, Troop Flag

Yoke Fiend - 41D

Battlekit: Trench Club, Trench Club

Yoke Fiend - 41D

Battlekit: Trench Club, Trench Club

Wretched - 27D

Battlekit: Trench Knife, Trench Knife, Petals of the Blood Roses

Wretched - 27D

Battlekit: Trench Knife, Trench Knife, Petals of the Blood Roses

Final Thoughts

Pride does not exactly play differently than most other Court lists do. Your lists will usually act like more of a refinement of the classic Big Three lists, making each of them into the most powerful and dangerous versions of themselves. Your elites can be fantastically lethal and extremely difficult to kill if played correctly and that only gets more true in campaign games where you have access to the best Glory Items of the faction. Your heavy lifting will be done by your Elites, everyone else is there to sit bodies on objectives and support your star players by any means.

Embrace your clear and objective greatness. Let nothing stand before you. Aura Farm. And rest assured that if they impossible happens and you do lose a game, it's all a part of your master plan and you clearly meant for it to occur so you can set up your future victories. For the Duke of Petals.

title: "We took a huge risk": how luck, tenacity, and lockdown made the wargame Eldfall Chronicles
content:
Eldfall Chronicles feels like it appeared overnight, suddenly showing up in American hobby stores after distributors caught wind of a hot new skirmish wargame with gorgeous miniatures that had grown up quietly in Slovenia. I spoke to Žiga Gantar, co-creator of the Eldfall Chronicles universe, and CEO and creative director of publisher Freecompany, to discover how it came to be.

"I started working on Eldfall when I was studying in Japan", Gantar says, enrolled on a Masters degree in East Asian studies alongside his now-fiancée Tjaša Gaber. "I couldn't play many wargames because I was away from home, so I started working on my own".

Eldfall Chronicles' origins

Work started with the setting, the world of Calad. "History is in general my hobby," Gantar says, "in my home university I spent a lot of time studying European history", and while in Japan he "spent a lot of time studying culture, history, not just Japanese history, Chinese as well, Korean as well". This is the origin for Eldfall's setting, a fantasy world with distinctly East Asian influences where "everything is intermingling, cultures are cross-pollinating".

Gantar and Gaber hadn't long returned from Japan when COVID hit, and "university kind of wasn't a thing anymore". "Me and my fiancée decided If there's ever going to be a time to work on a game, it's now". "Tjaša predominantly went into graphic design, writing, things like that - she's been writing most of the lore for us". Gantar focused on world building and illustration. "It was quite a journey going from miniature painting and sketching on paper to full-on digital art".

Before COVID restrictions had fully lifted "we started putting our own money into getting the first minis made, opening a company, stuff like that"… "I started working with 3D sculptors to design things, art directing". He admits "we took a huge risk".

Eldfall's miniatures are beautifully designed, though the style isn't exactly to my taste; they give me the vibe of characters in a high budget Chinese MMO created in the Unreal engine, and I tell Gantar as much. "Definitely some of the influence comes from there", he says, "when I was younger MMOs were the thing. On top of that I'm a huge fan of games like The Witcher and the From SoftwareGames, everything from Dark Souls, Sekiro, Bloodborne, Elden Ring, those gritty aesthetics".

I can see his point. The Western-coded factions, like the Helian League, remind me of Eastern media representations of Western fantasy archetypes, from Berserk, to Dark Souls, to the Japanese book covers for the Game of Thrones series. The studio also aims to make its miniatures more realistically proportioned than other wargames. "A lot of wargames go one to four, maybe one to five head to body ratio - we often go with one to six, one to seven".

Unicool miniatures

While Eldfall miniatures aren't excessively busy with details, the details they do have are extremely finely rendered - they're more detailed than I can easily paint. That wouldn't be possible without a high quality casting process; it feels a bit miraculous that two first-time game developers with no experience of model production managed to find one. "It was a mixture of tenacity and luck", Gantar says. "We tried a number [of manufacturers], at least 12 that we exchanged materials with, checked what they can do, how helpful they are".

It was around the time of the first Eldfall Chronicles Kickstarter campaign in 2021 that the team was contacted by Unicool Plastic Manufacturing. "From the get-go, they were way more helpful as people than many other manufacturers". The firm's chief engineer "offered to test out a new material with us", and after some back and forth tests to develop the specifications, "we were the first game on the market using Unicool Hard Plastic, or Unicast as they now call it, for our whole range of models".

I've built Unicast miniatures from both Eldfall Chronicles and Corvus Belli's Warcrow; it's light, strong, is similar in hardness and flexibility to HIPS, and it captures fine detail like traditional cold pour resins. "It's only been evolving", Gantar enthuses, "before there were some problems with the material, like bent parts - especially with long thin weapons, and we really like to make realistic weapons - it pushed the Unicool guys to work on the material, and the latest version is really awesome".

Skirmish and dungeon crawl

Eldfall Chronicles has grown into quite an unusual product line. There are two main branches - the dungeon crawler board games, such as the existing Northern Winds set or the currently-crowdfunding Apocrypha, and then the skirmish wargame. The miniatures are cross compatible between the two lines, and while individual minis aren't cheap, starting to play the skirmish game is, because a playable party consists of just four figures.

"Obviously we want you to buy more miniatures," Gantar chuckles, "But at the same time, we wanted to bring the starting point low, so anyone can start playing the game". I've not played enough of Eldfall to give it a scored review, but my first impressions are very promising. There's a strong sense of characters having detailed and defined roles within the party, needing to coordinate their limited activations to achieve the mission. With every model so specialized it's very important to consider the capabilities of your opponent's force, as you can run into very hard counters for certain strategies that you'll have to think your way around.

"We play a lot of RPGs", Gantar says, "I spent a lot of time with things like Divinity, so I really like the whole idea of isometric exploration, and that's kind of the vibe I also wanted for Eldfall: I wanted people to make their own parties, outfit them however you like with upgrades and things like that". The model pool for list building is broad, since many models work in multiple factions and there are plenty of mercenaries, but so far the dedicated list for each individual faction is quite shallow.

More minis are coming: "in the future we are doing more reinforcement packs, more new factions, new faction starters". Fans are already keen to get play modes that will allow them to use more of their collection in a game, though Gantar doesn't want to do this just by lifting the points cap: "it would just bloat it up, you don't get any added value from it".

Variant playmodes are a big part of Eldfall; about a third of the range is made up of monsters which are controlled by AI and show up in cooperative or semi-co-operative missions. "PVE is huge for some communities, there's a lot of people who don't want to straight up compete", Gantar says, adding that Tjaša is one of them. "She likes to play things in an adventure sense, like together we're going after a monster". It's another aspect of the game that comes from Gantar and the wider team's love of RPGs.

Eldfall Chronicles Apocrypha

Freecompany's current focus is its second dungeon crawler board game, Apocrypha, currently seeking funds on Gamefound. There's no need to own Northern Winds to be able to use this one, and while it's set up for co-op with four players, it includes a true solo mode, allowing you to play through it with a single hero.

The core version of Apocrypha is a little slimmer than its big brother Northern Winds; to make it more cost friendly for board gamers it swaps out a lot of miniatures for cardboard standees. A pledge comes in at just under $100, with four hero minis and a hulking great boss. There are options to spend a lot more and get a lot more miniatures, of course, and every model has skirmish game rules as well.

Given the recent spate of controversies around delayed and incomplete crowdfunding campaigns, I ask Gantar how complete the project is and what remains to be done after crowdfunding closes. "The project is around 90 to 95 percent finished behind the scenes", he replies, "we are in the process of [doing layout] and editing for production, also finalizing miniatures, optimizing them, things like that". "We're just patching up holes, seeing where some lore can be added, or if we need to remove some lore somewhere because it tells too much", he adds.

Despite the bevy of cool miniatures coming in this release, Gantar says "for me personally, it's really interesting from the story point of view". "You have a monumental grand library in the Sand Kingdoms; beneath it there's a sealed away section, and things have started to stir there, knowledge that shouldn't have been written has started to appear in those sealed archives".

The entity known as the Librarian cannot enter the archives, so they've tasked a group of mortals to delve in for them and return with these apocrypha. "Our party of heroes have a hidden goal; a part of their party went missing 17 years back, in a previous prospecting expedition into the archives, and they are now back to see what happened".

In terms of new gameplay, Gantar thinks the team have done very good work with "a really cool taint and party progression mechanic". There are other parties in the archives who "can steal loot from you if you're too slow, if you take too much time doing side quests". That gives a sense of urgency to your delves. You'll also have to manage the growing taint that afflicts your party as they're exposed to profane mana. "Those were kind of difficult things [to design], but also surprising in a really good way how they turned out".

The Gamefound campaign for Eldfall Chronicles: Apocrypha is open until November 24.

Meanwhile there's a growing chance you'll be able to acquire the existing range from your friendly local game store. When I spoke to Gantar he had just returned from the colossal SPIEL convention in Essen, Germany. "I was really busy with business-to-business meetings", he says, "most of the time I spent in my small cubicle office on the booth", talking to European, American, and even South Korean distributors. "SPIEL was quite a step up from last year", he reflects, "we've started being recognized by other players in the community - it's really nice".

There are a few Eldfall players in the Wargamer Discord community if you'd like to find some more knowledgeable nerds to talk about the game - and if you've painted any of the miniatures, please share them in our mini-painting channel!

title: WTC Opens Its Books as Belül Controversy Continues
content:
The ongoing saga around the World Team Championship (WTC) and former organizer Işık Belül continued this week as both groups exchanged additional comments on the 2025 Leoben event’s finances and the decision to end Belül’s role. The exchange follows the WTC’s November 10 statement, which disputed Belül’s October account and released a comparison of the initial Leoben budget outline against what the current team describes as the reported result. You can find our reporting on Belül's initial statement here.

For anyone looking for a quick recap of the story so far and an introduction who these people are and why this matters, look below.

A Quick Primer - Click to Expand

The WTC is the World Team Championship, an independent events organizer formerly run by Tom Adriany, Işık Belül, François Lesestre, Christian Lord, Fernando Kerubus, Michael Banz, and Neil Kerr. The WTC is responsible for running the annual Warhammer 40k tournament of the same name as part of a larger event that often includes other games, such as Kill Team, X-Wing, and Age of Sigmar (notably a singles event and not the world team championships for that game). The event is normally held in late summer, and in past years has typically been held in Mechelen, Belgium. In 2025 the event was relocated to Leoben, Austria under the guidance of Işık Belül and reportedly lost money due to a number of factors. In 2026 the event was moved back to Mechelen and Işık Belül was removed from his position at the WTC. The two sides have had public disagreements since his removal, with each claiming the other is responsible for the loss of revenue in 2025 and is unfit to run the organization.

In Belül’s original statement, the WTC co-founder argued that remaining WTC management is “unfit for purpose” and urged team captains to consider moving the event. He linked his removal to ongoing disagreements over a business relationship with Belül’s company centering around terrain for the event, the failed 2024 effort to form an Austrian company (which he contends led to further loss of revenue from missed state subsidies), and demands from other WTC managers that he publicly take accountability for perceived failures of the 2025 Leoben event in a manner he rejected. He also claimed that terrain-licensing revenue and certain sponsorships stayed in Belgium rather than supporting Leoben, and that Kill Team and X-Wing were effectively subsidized by the 40K event.

On November 10, the WTC released its own statement, signed by Tom Adriany, Francois, Christian, Fernando, Michael Banz, and former WTC organizer Neil Kerr. In that statement, the group listed conflicts of interest, a lack of accountability, a breach of trust related to Leoben financial reporting, and interpersonal issues as the basis for ending their working relationship with Belül. They disputed that the absence of Kill Team and X-Wing was the main cause of the Leoben shortfall and released a spreadsheet comparing the initial budget (which projected a “real expected profit” range of €75,000–€125,000) to later figures. The statement described the comparison as the team’s assessment of Belül’s outline. It is important to note that what WTC released in the November 10 statement is not an independent review, and the underlying actuals have not been released alongside it. Kerr left the organization in 2023 and has had no formal role for three years; neither the statement nor subsequent comments have explained his inclusion as a signatory.

In comment provided to Tabletop Battles, Adriany claimed the net reported loss from Leoben was “5,000–6,000 euros” and confirmed that this figure does not match any total in the released spreadsheets. He described these documents as incomplete and “quickly hobbled [sic] together when WTC leadership insisted on some accountability from Isik's end” once they heard of a deficit against the earlier profit projection and after the roughly €26,000 bar budget had been removed from the event financial reporting. Adriany confirmed that the “conclusions” column in the comparison spreadsheet is annotated by the WTC team, written in response to a financial debrief shared by the captains council, rather than material from Belül. No calculation supporting the €5,000–€6,000 figure has been provided.

One major point of focus is the event’s second weekend, during which the WTC had planned to host other games and events, including Kill Team, X-Wing, an Age of Sigmar singles event, and a painting competition. Adriany attributed the plan to fill the hall with roughly 400 people across multiple systems to Belül and a collaborator named Kevin, stating that Games Workshop leadership had not requested it (there is a notion that the 40k publisher might have requested some level of exclusivity for the teams event). Notably, these events did not occur - Kill Team and X-Wing ran separate events in Mechelen, while the Age of Sigmar event and painting competition were scrapped entirely. According to Adriany, the events that actually ran that weekend were small— “an 18 man beer and pretzels doubles event, a 59 player WH40K singles event, and an 18-man AOS event” —and he argued that Kill Team and X-Wing would have seen similarly low turnout if forced to Leoben. He said the side events that did occur that weekend contributed roughly as much as those systems would have.

In response, Belül has prepared a lengthy point-by-point reply, which he provided to Tabletop Battles in response to a request for comment. He claims he already accepted responsibility for the Leoben outcome in the “Lessons Learned” document sent to management and the Captains Council at the end of March, including failing to recognize in time that the side events would not succeed. He maintains that Kill Team and X-Wing “did have part in the WTC 2025 financial loss, not the entire thing but definitely partially,” particularly because the Austrian company was never formed (Belül claims that not forming the company meant losing out on a large amount of revenue in government subsidies), and partially because the organization carried dual sets of costs. He claims that the decision to hand bar revenue and costs to the venue was made collectively in a meeting during the event year, with any profits to be donated to a future WTC organization. Belül primarily lists undercharged tickets (team tickets cost €900 in 2025 once lunches were removed - on which see more below - versus €1,800 in 2026), the absence of Kill Team and X-Wing, cancelled side events, and unrealized government subsidies as the key contributing factors to the Leoben event generating a loss.

The spreadsheets, however, provide a significant amount of data that can be used to interrogate some of the claims and counter-claims. Although on the surface there are eye-catching cost overruns and failures to realise revenues, there are also several places where the WTC’s presentation does not align cleanly with the underlying financial data. The net loss on ticket sales compared to budget is €13,845, which the WTC team attributes to the Warmaster GT underperforming and the failure of the AoS and painting events to launch, while claiming that Kill Team and X-Wing revenue was compensated for by other ticket sales. However, the lost revenue from those two events is projected at €13,450 - almost exactly the net shortfall. The secondary hotel position shows a budgeted net contribution of roughly €9,000 becoming a €15,000 cost. Public hotel-reservation announcements made by the WTC for the second week during the lead-up to Leoben show substantial bookings at Hotel Kongress and a sold-out Living Campus, which stand in contrast to the spreadsheets’ description of secondary hotel income as having not materialized.

WTC Leoben Hotel Booking Announcement, April 24 2025
WTC Leoben Living Campus Announcement, May 16, 2025

The expenses spreadsheet itemizes costs by hotel, with costs for the Living Campus listed as rising by €9,000, and Hotel Kongress incurring zero cost, which would still have left a profitable overall position thanks to €90,000 hotel income. What mostly wiped this out were costs from a third accommodation option, Hotel Kindler, where an expected €9,000 cost became €15,000, and no income is logged, making for an overall €24,000 loss compared to budget. The contemporaneous hotel booking updates simply show this hotel as “available” where both Kongress and Living Campus were filling up (with the Living Campus later listed as sold out), even for the week of the 40K WTC itself. This plausibly suggests over-optimistic projections for room sales, but it’s also far more explicable than it’s presented as in the WTC accounts.

This also highlights the potential compounding effects of lower player numbers. Even if the separate Kill Team and X-Wing events held in Mechelen were profitable, lost revenue from the hotel bookings and additional venue costs strengthens the case that keeping these events separate hurt the Leoben event. However, there are also indications that the impact of some logistical challenges were simply underestimated; the player shuttle, budgeted at €4,000 with a note that it might be fully subsidized, is listed at €11,630.

The treatment of food and player/team lunches is particularly difficult to reconcile. The original budget listed 40K team tickets at €1,200, and the income analysis shows that lunches were essentially charged at €15 per-person, per-diem. For teams of nine people (assuming the inclusion of a coach), once lunch was included the loaded price would have been approximately €1,740, but the event only charged €1,350 for those tickets, a total difference of roughly €16,000 based on the 42 teams which attended. The WTC annotations in the comparison notes that ticket prices were lowered because of the high projected profit; neither side has identified who made that decision.

As a result of the decision for lunch costs to be folded into ticket prices, the comparison then shows both higher ticket income and also a large catering expense. The WTC’s analysis does not make clear that the ticket revenue is not being compared on a like for like basis, and presents the €30,000 of “missed income” for food sales without adequately explaining that this has been separately accounted for in the ticket sales section. The document’s explanation that ticket overperformance for the core 40k teams event offset the projected Kill Team and X-Wing shortfall is therefore hard to substantiate, as it appears that the claimed overperformance is primarily driven by changing where the “food sales” revenue is accounted for.

Belül has separately noted that team ticket prices were lower in 2025 than in 2026 once lunches were removed. Decisions on lunch also appear to have some overlap with the decision to allow the venue to take on the operation and profits from the bar, a major point of contention between the accounts. The WTC account presents this as a major loss, while Belül indicates that costs of operating a bar often overrun, making the loss less impactful (though the original estimate presents it as a potential significant revenue source). However, delegating the food to the venue appears to have worked very well for the event - the financials indicate they were simply charged a unit cost of €13 per meal compared to the €15 they rolled into ticket prices; if that is accurate, it provided a small amount of headroom for staff catering, and seems to have flexibly adapted to the final player numbers. It does also again highlight that the comparison between tickets sold is not a like-for-like comparison; a significant contributor to the 40k overperformance against expected revenue were additional tickets for team staff, of which the majority of the cost was for catering.

For the WTC’s part, the initial budget outline itself contains multiple unsupported estimates, including a subsidy total of €21,250 accompanied by an unelaborated guess that the final amount would reach €30,000. Multiple line items are annotated as “Generous estimate from [past event]”, and one €500 cost line is labeled simply ‘thrash’ with a note that reads ‘dont ask.’ The WTC’s comparison document also lists €763 under miscellaneous costs for ‘Treatment for team,’ noted as massages for judges plus breakfasts, dinners, and lunches. Neither the WTC statement nor Belül’s reply explains the contractual relationship between Alpine Cup GmbH (the Austrian-domiciled company which we understand actually ran the event), the venue, and the WTC (which consists of two Belgian entities, a non-profit and a company), or which party ultimately bore responsibility for these results. The failed/stalled effort to form a WTC-controlled Austrian company is cited by Belül as a reason government subsidies did not materialize; the WTC statement does not address that timeline. It also appears to have made some degree of conflict of interest in the running of the event effectively inevitable without strong contractual controls addressing Belül’s dual position with the WTC and Alpine Cup.

The materials released to-date show that Belül’s original budget outline contained significant, overly optimistic estimates and that the side events for the second weekend which he projected did not materialize; these are outcomes for which Belül has accepted responsibility in the Lessons Learned document. The final stated financial position is also not easy to reconcile with the figures in the spreadsheet. At the same time, the WTC’s comparison spreadsheet and November 10 statement present the results in ways that do not align cleanly with the underlying financials provided - most notably in the treatment of the Kill Team and X-Wing revenue, the food and ticket figures, and the secondary hotels - while failing to address the lack of documented oversight on key decisions (such as the ‘don’t ask’ line item), the failure to form the Austrian company in time for expected subsidies, and the related-party structure through which the event was run. The net effect is an account that assigns primary responsibility to Belül while the released figures and process gaps indicate broader failures of planning and supervision.

Captains considering future hosting decisions still lack a complete final accounting for 2026. On November 3 the WTC announced that it had concluded the bid process for 2027 and would begin negotiations with Games Workshop to act as a hosting partner (note: These negotiations are being initiated by the WTC - Games Workshop has not made an offer or bid to host); should those negotiations not succeed in the next six to eight weeks, the bid would go to Mechelen. In the captains’ ranking, 34 of 45 participating nations placed the Games Workshop option first.

Tabletop Battles continues to monitor this story and will update this piece as appropriate. If you would like to reach out to us on or off the record, e-mail us at contact@tabletopbattles.com with the subject line "WTC."

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!
