title: [40k] Ruleshammer 11th Edition: Adeptus Custodes
content:
Welcome to 11th Ruleshammer 11th Edition: Custodes a tour of the of their rules and interactions that I’ve been asked about! If you have any Custodes questions you’d like to see answered in a future update to this article please do send them via this form! 

Changelog

  • Published: 2026-11-13

Current Q&A

When do Martial Ka’tahs get declared used?

Whilst mostly straight forward there is a bit of confusion I’ve seen regarding how Martial Ka'tahs are declared and then used. Let’s start by looking at the rule itself.

At the start of your Command phase, friendly ADEPTUS CUSTODES units with this ability are readied. While a friendly unit is readied, you can select one of the ka’tah abilities presented below for that unit to use. If you do, that unit is no longer readied.

Each ka’tah ability will tell you when that ka’tah ability can be used, and the effects that ka’tah ability has on the unit using it.

We recommend placing a token next to each readied unit, removing it when that unit is no longer readied.

It is easy (I think) to read this and come to the conclusion that all aspects of this rule take place in the Command Phase; at least, that’s what I thought on my first read of the rule. Instead, however, it’s more nuanced than that. One part of this rule always happens in the Command Phase: All the units with this ability become “readied.” That always happens.

What you are required to do next however depends on which Martial Ka'tahs you want to use. If you want to use the Conservai Ka'tah then you need to use it next, during the command phase. That’s because the WHEN clause for that Ka'tah is “your Command phase.” The others, though, have WHEN clauses that all occur in different phases; you don’t need to declare these until you want to use them and readied units stay readied until a Martial Ka'tah is used on the unit.

Can I declare a Martial Ka'tah and then use Master of Ka'tahs to re-ready my unit to then have two active simultaneously?

Yes, I think so. The ability causes a non-readied unit to become readied again.

Master of Ka’tahs (Once per battle round, per unit): If this unit is not readied, you can use this ability. If you do, this unit is readied.

This ability is not limited to any specific phase or triggering moment; it can just be used on a not-readied unit. There’s perhaps some debate you could have on when a unit stops being readied but I think it stops being readied when a Martial Ka’tah is used on the unit, rather than when it’s resolved. Otherwise the Start of Phase ones would mean the units are potentially still readied for a significant amount of time while waiting for that ability to happen. So if you were in the Fight Phase and used the Dacatarai Ka’tah on your unit, used at the start of the Fight phase, then use Master of Ka’tahs to ready the unit again, and subsequently declare Kaptaris.

When do Martial Ka’tahs end?

There’s a general rule that if a rule doesn’t state an end timing then they last until the end of the phase.

Persisting Rule Effects 01.02.02

...

If a rule or effect given to a unit does not specify how long it is active for, it is only active for the phase in which it was given.

There are other instances where this rule is relevant throughout the Codex; several of the stratagems don’t specify when their effects end. Sorry, using Honoured Interred on a Dreadnought doesn’t give it that aura all game; just until the end of the phase it was used in.

What does a “Once Per Army” Upgrade mean?

There are several such Upgrades in the Custodes Codex, such as Memento Moritoi or Augury Uplink, available to Dreadnoughts in armies using the Might of Moritoi Detachment. Whilst the main effect associated with the Upgrade tag is that you can take them several times in the same army, that’s actually just part of several rules associated with the tag.

Upgrades: Some enhancements are tagged with ’Upgrade’. Unlike other enhancements:

    • These can be given to non-CHARACTER units.
    • You can include up to three of the same Upgrade in your army (the second and third instances of the same Upgrade do not count towards the total number of enhancements in your army, but you must still spend the stated points cost each time).

So while they can’t benefit from the second effect from this rule, the first Upgrade still counts towards your enhancement limit and their Codex rule limits you to one of them in total, the Upgrade tag is the rule that allows these upgrades to be given to non-CHARACTER units such as all of the Custodes Dreadnoughts.

Unleash the Lions

One of the more thematic stratagems for Custodes, but it obviously causes a number of questions. We aren’t entirely blind on some of them thanks to the recent Warhammer World Championship FAQ released this week, but that document specifies that these answers are not errata or FAQ and currently only apply for the World Championship. Let's look at them one by one and see if they line up with expectations from the rules as written, giving some indication perhaps of if these answers will stick around and be added to the 40k App.

Does using the stratagem destroy the unit it’s used on?

Q: When I target a unit with the Unleash the Lions stratagem, is that unit destroyed?

A: No.

This is pretty important because otherwise using this stratagem would potentially cause the unit to count for mission objectives.

Has the unit I targeted with Unleash the Lions left the battlefield?

Q: When I target a unit with the Unleash the Lions stratagem, does that unit leave the battlefield?

A: Yes.

I’m not clear on what this actually does in 11th edition. They’ve removed a lot of the distinction Warhammer 40k used to have between being “destroyed” and “leaving the battlefield.” I guess there’s no harm in clarifying that the unit isn’t on the battlefield any more, though.

Do persisting effects pass to the new units?

Q: When I target a unit with the Unleash the Lions stratagem, do persisting rules effects pass to the new units (e.g. Fulgrim's Daemonic Poisons ability)?

A: No.

Honestly, this one is probably one of the more disappointing rulings in the FAQ doc for me. I can see the logical reasoning that the stratagem creates three new units out of the models that used to make up one other unit, so effects on that unit don’t pass along. Flavour-wise though this feels quite gamey; that’s not a strong rebuttal by any means, but I can see why people would be disappointed by it. People want the units they cover in Squigs to remain covered in Squigs for as long as Gork (or Mork) intended without wiggling out from the Squigs on a technicality that essentially boils down to:

“Oh that wasn’t me you covered in Squigs; it was my identical twin brother, who just left the battlefield, honest.”

Do the new units get to use “once per battle abilities” even if their original unit has used them?

Q: When I target a unit with the Unleash the Lions stratagem, do the new units have their 'once per battle' abilities even if the original unit used those abilities?

A: Yes.

Honestly surprised by this one as well, considering it’s the same technicality that causes this to be true. I appreciate them having an answer on it, but I don’t think it’s unfair to expect “once per battle” abilities to be usable once per battle.

Custodes Official FAQs

This section will list official GW FAQs when GW shares some. I have not included Q&A from the World Championship rules update here based on its status as a single event document.

These responses are provided by the Warhammer studio and, while many rulings may be adopted as official rules updates in the future, they are currently only considered valid for the World Championships. As a result they will not be appearing in the Warhammer 40,000 app before the event.

That's all for this weeks Ruleshammer; if you have some questions you think I should cover in the future though please do send them via this form! 

Have any other questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

Pokemon sets FAQ

The list above tells you every set released in Pokémon TCG history - but there's more to the story of Pokémon cards than that! Read on for answers to some of the most common questions about sets, to help you get a handle on the hobby.

How many Pokémon sets are there?

As of January 2026, there have been 130 English language Pokémon sets that were legal to use in organized play at the time they were printed.

The pace of Pokémon sets picked up last year, with a huge bubble of fan hype and interest for releases around January 2025's Prismatic Evolutions, and shows no sign of abating. In fact, this year (2026) is the 30th anniversary of Pokémon TCG's original launch, so there's every chance the hype train could speed up over the coming months!

If you want to store a large collection of cards, our guide to Pokémon card sizes has their dimensions and weight so you can work out exactly how much space you'll need.

How many Pokémon sets are released every year?

Around three to four Regular Pokémon sets are released each year - usually accompanied by two to four special sets and smaller promotional packs.

For example, in 2025 there were seven sets in total, including:

  • Four regular sets - Journey Together, Destined Rivals, Mega Evolution, and Phantasmal Flames.
  • Three special sets - Prismatic Evolutions, White Flare and Black Bolt.

What are the different types of Pokémon sets?

There are three main types of Pokémon TCG sets:

  1. Regular sets: The TCG's mainline releases, Regular sets are the 'tentpole' events of each season, releasing at roughly regular intervals each year with a large number of cards. Regular sets are normally available in quite a few different product types, including booster boxes of 36 ten-card booster packs.
  2. Special sets: Also sometimes called 'Special Collections', these sets generally have a smaller overall card list and a specific theme that underpins their most prominent cards. Special sets don't get booster boxes and are normally sold in Elite Trainer Boxes (ETBs) and small promotional packs like Binder Collections.
  3. Mini-sets: A catch-all term for all smaller set releases that don't merit the 'Special Collection' label, but are still a distinct collection of new or reprinted cards. These usually come in their own seasonal or promotional packs, like the three-card Trick or Trade mini packs released around Halloween, or promo tins.

And - for now - that's it for our guide to Pokémon TCG sets! If you've got a favorite to support, or just want to join the hype about upcoming sets, come hop into the Pokémon TCG discussion in our Discord community! Chances are we're also salivating over the latest chase SIR, too.

Alternatively, we've got lots more Pokémon TCG guides to help you along - we can even help you answer the twin age-old questions - how many Pokémon are there, and how many Pokémon cards are there?

title: All 13 DnD damage types explained
content:
Thirteen different DnD damage types define the many ways you can slash, freeze, burn, zap, shatter, or otherwise dispatch your fiendish foes. Everyone has a favorite (No? Just me?), but hot takes aren't going to help you survive in battle. This guide is for anyone who wants to really understand the damage system in D&D. Knowledge is power, and it might just save your skin.

This guide covers key spells for each damage type, as well as monsters who are resistant or weak to each. Once you're armed with all that handy info, head to our DnD classes and DnD races guides for more tactical tips.

For now, let's get studious:

DnD Damage TypeExampleStrong againstWeak against
PiercingSpears, bitesRakshasa (if magical)Swarms, Ghosts, Treants
BludgeoningMaces, unarmed strikesSkeletonsSwarms, Ghosts, Treants
SlashingSwords, talonsNoneSwarms, Ghosts
ColdCone of Cold, Ice Devil's spearSalamandersLiches, Storm Giants, Fiends
FireBurning Hands, Salamander's tailIce Mephits, Scarecrows, TreantsSalamanders, Fiends, some Oozes
LightningStorm Giant's Lightning BoltNoneAir Elementals, Liches, some Fiends
ThunderShatter, ThunderwaveEarth ElementalsAir Elementals, some Undead
PoisonStings and bitesNoneAssassins, loads of Fiends, Elementals, and Undead
AcidAcid Arrow, Black Dragon's Breath WeaponNoneBlack Dragons, some Golem, Mimics
NecroticWight's Life Drain attackNoneMost Undead
RadiantAngel's weapon attackShadows, Shadow DemonsCelestials
ForceMagic MissileNoneNone!
PsychicPsionic Blast, Mind Flayer's powersFlumphsConstructs and Aberrations

Piercing

You duck the Giant's club, then loose a crossbow bolt into its ankle.

The first three DnD damage types are what you might call the Physical damage types. They're some of the most common forms of damage in the game, dished out by all common weapons. That means every class that regularly uses a weapon, from the Fighter to the DnD Rogue, will make use of these damage types.

Piercing damage specifically refers to stabbing, puncturing wounds, of the kind dealt by spears, bows, and rapiers. Like the other physical damage types, there are almost no creatures that are vulnerable to piercing damage, but also few that actively resist it. You'll mainly have trouble fighting swarms of little biting things, or ethereal creatures like Ghosts.

Interestingly, the tiger demon Rakshaha is vulnerable to piercing damage, but only when it's dealt by a magical weapon, and only if that weapon is wielded by a hero of a good alignment.

Piercing damage is also commonly dished out by monsters, from spear-wielding humanoids to beasts attacking with bites, horns, spikes, or thorns.

Bludgeoning

You deliver the unruly drunk a staggering knock-out blow, then whack him with a stool for good measure.

Bludgeoning damage refers to blunt force trauma, of the kind delivered by maces and warhammers, or a fist. It's the default for unarmed combat, so a DnD Monk will make immense use of this damage type, but again this is one type that no player will have trouble accessing.

Bludgeoning is arguably the strongest of the physical damage types. Similar monsters resist it, but unlike slashing or piercing, a few common monsters are vulnerable to getting bludgeoned, most notably Skeletons.

Slashing

You scream out as the Owlbear's claw catches your side, raking across your flesh.

Slashing damage is the third physical damage type, and it refers to cutting attacks of the kind delivered by a sword or an axe, or by a monster's claws. While few creatures have vulnerabilities, there are many that have resistances to multiple damage types, and then one damage type missing.

So for instance, Treants are not vulnerable to slashing damage, but they are resistant to bludgeoning and piercing. In a sense, they have a sort of pseudo-vulnerability to slashing by way of being resistant to other weapons. It certainly makes sense that a tree person would find an axe more concerning than a rapier.

Cold

A blast of freezing air jets forth from your fingertips, encasing the goblin in ice.

We've now departed from the most common DnD damage types and are now looking at damage that's most often dealt by magic.

Cold damage is a little less intuitive to imagine than fire, but it's still pretty straightforward. It refers to the pain and damage caused by sudden exposure to immensely cold temperatures. You'll probably need a spellcasting class or a magic item to make use of it.

In terms of spells, the DnD Wizard gets Cone of Cold, delivering a huge amount of AoE cold damage. Meanwhile, the DnD Warlock gets a fantastic defensive cold spell in Armor of Agathys, gaining temporary hit points and dealing cold damage to those who come too near. Monstrous sources of the damage type include Elementals, Yetis, and frosty White Dragon breath.

There are a few monsters that are weak to cold damage, most of which are some kind of fire monster like the Salamander. But on the flip side, a large number of monsters say the cold never bothered them (anyway). If a creature looks wintry and ice-clad it might be totally immune, while most fiends are resistant to cold damage.

Fire

Ushering patrons out of the burning inn, your arms are singed by a sudden conflagration.

Fire damage is self-explanatory: we all know what fire is and how it damages stuff. In terms of dishing it out, there are plenty of spells to draw from, and if you want to be throwing Fireballs nonstop, we suggest the Evocation Wizard could be right for you.

However, unlike cold or lightning, you can also harness fire using mundane equipment. If you're out of spell slots, oil flasks and a tinderbox may come in clutch to turn up the heat on a burnable monster.

Fire damage is a rather mixed bag. It has a higher number of vulnerable monsters than any other damage type (wooden or ice-based enemies beware) but more monsters resist fire than any other damage type, barring poison. In particular, if you're taking a trip to the Nine Hells, leave your fire scrolls at home. Fiends will have a field day with fire-reliant PCs.

Lightning

The foolish Bugbear jabs the artificer's machine with his knife, leading to a flash and the smell of singed hair.

Lightning damage refers to harm caused by high-voltage electricity, which you're unlikely to come across through normal means unless you stand on a tower in full plate mail during a storm. So it's to spells we turn once again, where the lightning spells range from small cantrips like Shocking Grasp to big hitters like Chain Lightning.

In terms of high-electricity monsters you're likely to meet, the Blue Dragon unleashes lightning on its foes, while Storm Giants can hurl Lightning Bolts from range. There aren't any monsters particularly vulnerable to lightning damage, but it's not a very resisted damage type either. Most monsters that resist lightning also resist other common types like fire and cold damage.

Thunder

The Shatter spell releases an eardrum-rupturing sound, cracking the crystal wall.

Not to be confused with the previous entry, Thunder damage refers to harm caused by an intense shockwave of sound. In fact, it was known as 'sonic damage' in fourth edition.

It's one of the stronger damage types in D&D, having only a few resistant or immune monsters, and being strong against Earth Elementals. It's also quite rare that you'll come up against it. If you want to avoid thunder damage, be careful not to piss off any Djinn.

Poison

As your stomach lurches, you glance at your goblet in horror.

Poison damage comes from contact with or ingestion of harmful substances. There aren't that many spells that inflict it, and in fact, this is a damage type that seems more likely to come from a monster, whether a serpent, Green Dragon, or countless other stinging or fanged monsters.

Unfortunately for those who do take the trouble to pick up a poison spell, poison is one of the least effective damage types, resisted by an enormous portion of the Monster Manual. Anything with a strong Constitution or no blood is likely to shrug off poison attacks.

Acid

'I'm mellltinng', shrieks the Lich, sinking slowly into the deadly pool.

Now we're getting to the good stuff. Unlike poison, which generally has to be ingested or injected to cause harm, Acid damage comes from corrosive, dissolving substances that are harmful to the touch.

It's a good DnD damage type because it's highly consistent. Though there are no monsters with acid vulnerability, very few monsters are immune to acid's (I was going to say charms, but that's not it) power. Acid does struggle against some inanimate creatures like the Mimic, but overall spells like Melf's Acid Arrow are reliable favorites. Along with fire, acid is also a damn near requisite for fighting Trolls.

Radiant

A beam of holy light reduces the Vampire to nothing but dust.

The next few damage types are the hardest to imagine, because they don't correspond with anything you'll encounter in the real world. Radiant damage, for instance, refers to the burning power of holy light. While some might expect it to be effective against all unholy, Undead monsters, it's only the darkness-dwelling shadows that actually fear the light.

While the special damage types we've seen so far are mainly the purview of the party's Wizard or DnD Sorcerer, radiant damage is more likely to be wielded by a Cleric or Paladin. You're unlikely to run into much that resists it, though if you're waging war on heaven, there are some strange celestial creatures that will only take half damage.

Necrotic

The wight's chilling touch causes your skin to wither.

The flipside of radiant damage, Necrotic damage is best described as 'unholy'. Rather than Devils though, it's specifically related to the Undead, who are both its main users and the monster type you don't want to target. Interestingly, while some Undead are resistant or immune to necrotic attacks, not all of them are. You're probably better off hitting a Skeleton or Zombie with Chill Touch than slashing it with your sword.

While it's often associated with evil, there's nothing that dictates that a practitioner of necromancy or user of necrotic damage has to be bad or good.

Force

Your bolt of pure magic impacts with the Hook Horror at speed.

Force damage is a somewhat indescribable category that's given to magical projectiles and weapons. Spiritual Weapon and Eldritch Blast are common examples.

Force is often described as the best DnD damage type, and while that honorific is largely going to depend on what you're fighting and how many dice you're rolling, there's no denying that it is effective. There are no creatures that are resistant to force damage, not one. At the same time, none are particularly vulnerable to it (even the Helmed Horror, who was vulnerable in 2014 5e). If a monster doesn't seem to be taking enough damage from your regular spells, it's time to use the force.

Psychic

The Mind Flayer locks eyes with you and your head erupts in agony, unseeable tendrils wriggling into your brain.

One of the creepiest ways to hurt stuff in DnD, Psychic damage refers to damaging effects that alter or harm your very mind. Inflicted by some of the spookiest monsters like the Banshee or Mind Flayer, psychic damage presumably feels like the mother of all migraines. If D&D had a sanity stat, this is the damage type that would deplete it.

Psychic is another very reliable damage type, with few monsters resisting spells like the DnD Bard's Vicious Mockery. There are some creatures, such as mindless beings like Constructs, that will be completely immune, however.

That's all the damage types there are. Now go forth and lay waste, and make sure you come join the free Wargamer Discord community to tell us which monsters you merked. Or, for more rules explainers, here's all you need to know about DnD languages and DnD level ups.

content:
Welcome back, Dear Reader, to my ongoing blog of hobby and competitive play progress through 2026. Last week I was doing some hobby work prepping for the Ettin RTT, hoping to get in a few practice games, both to refresh myself on the rules I'd be playing and to just get in some more Warhammer before the World Championships in December. I started the year off hot games-wise, but I've been very lax since July or so, mostly due to a lot more travel and work requirements.

Ok so first thing to note: This is a bad list. It's not good. Vindicators aren't great in 11th, and Land Raiders are also bad. But I have them, they're painted well, and I can work with them. In an ideal world I'd have at least five more Terminators, and a trio of Mutilators + Kravek Morne to round the group out. Huron and Terminators would be a fine combo if I could get another five but at the moment he's really here because he's painted. This is probably what I'm going to play at most of the Grand Narrative, because it's playably good but bad enough that I'm not liable to be accused of going too hard in the paint at an event where many people just don't play that much Warhammer.

As far as the units here go, there are three big unit threats: The Terminators with the Terminator Sorcerer, who are here to do a lot of bolter shots and drop Death Hex on an enemy unit, Bile with the unit of Chosen, Huron, and the Masters of the Maelstrom, and Huron with his unit of Legionaries, plus the Master of Executions with Touched by the Warp so they get the PSYKER keyword and better bolters. That's really the way I'm working here: I'm throwing out an assload of bolter shots at S6 AP-2 and sometimes Lethal Hits or Sustained Hits to take out targets. It's better than it looks, but it can't compete with Space Marines, who can just do that more efficiently and with better movement.

Cabal of Chaos here gets me +1 Strength on my ranged attacks with PSYKER units when I do a Dark Pact. There are also some great Stratagems in the Detachment to do mortals and heal dead models.

Veterans of the Long War gets me a second reactive move, plus that Focus of Hatred/Oath of moment ability helps make the Land Raider and the Vindicator actually playable.

My expectations were 2-1 and a best painted win. So I packed up and took my army over to Ettin games, which is a short enough drive that I can do an RTT and easily be home in time for dinner. For some reason the event was running 10-7 instead of 9-6, which was a bit annoying on the back end but I did appreciate the ability to sleep in a bit more than usual.

Round 1: vs. Connor's Ultramarines

Connor was playing Ultramarines and it's important to note that this list was not using the WCW FAQ, so this is also running Deathwatch Terminators with no nerfs. Good stuff - I'm cooked. Lists weren't made public for this event and I'm not going to go back and ask for them, so the key elements here are:

  • Guilliman
  • Calgar + Wardens + Bladeguard Veterans
  • Two Impulsors full of Eradicators
  • Incursors
  • Two units of Deathwatch Terminators
  • One unit of Heavy Intercessors
  • Phobos Librarian
  • Reivers

The Mission: Take and Hold vs. Take and Hold

This list is faster and meaner than mine. Its terminators are better by far, its Eradicators will kill my vehicles easily, and its big brick of Bladeguard Veterans are a nightmare. I had the first turn, so used the opportunity to push into Connor's Deployment Zone with Raiders on the left, charging his Heavy Intercessors and Impulsor. He was then able to intervene into them with his Deathwatch Terminators, but not with full attacks. My goal here was to try and tie him up an extra turn and block his movement on the right side, getting a good shot into his Calgar Brick by isolating them, hoping to kill them before anything else.

It kind of worked - The Raiders survived and pulled the Terminators back into Connor's deployment zone for a turn, but the Rhino full of Chosen got one-shot killed by the Impulsor full of melta, and the Chosen inside were charged and mostly wiped. I definitely misjudged the distance on those Bladeguard, but they also rolled a 6 to advance so I should have played it safer.

On my turn I pushed to the middle to try and wipe the Bladeguard and my Terminator Sorcerer promptly shit the bed and failed his Death Hex, which would be a brutal blow that meant the unit survived my all-out assault. I needed a decisive kill here and didn't get it, and as a result had to deal with being tied up at midtable while Guilliman pushed forward alive. I was sitting on about 45 VP at this point and ahead but as turn 3 rolled around it was clear I didn't have the gas left to keep it up and the second unit of Deathwatch Terminators hit my deployment zone.

The end result was just getting mostly tabled by the bottom of 3 by the insane amount of shooting left as I'd been forced to overcommit to killing the Calgar brick and didn't have the output I needed to kill anything else. The Eradicator Impulsors went more or less untouched and I didn't have the output I needed to kill them.

Result: 47-100, Loss

That was a brutal loss, and one I probably take even with the updates to Deathwatch Terminators. I just don't have the juice to compete with an army that's basically "mine, but way better on a per-unit basis." The good news is that now I'm in the loser bracket and liable to avoid nasty meta space marine lists.

I end up grabbing lunch with my on-again, off-again teammate, Chris Johnson, who's here playing a fun list that's substantially better than mine. We end up grabbing Portillo's for lunch - they just opened across the street and it's a solid lunch. Then it's back to the game mines for round 2.

Round 2: vs. Clay Sinclair's Chaos Space Marines

It's a mirror match! Well, kind of. Clay is running Veterans and Cabal, but with 20 terminators, two terminator sorcerers, Kravek Morne and a unit of Mutilators, Obliterators, and a Defiler. It's a more elite unit than mine, and one that'll struggle to spread out and do things. He's running one unit of Traitor Guardsmen and a unit of Beastmen, which give him some cool flexibility and forward OC but cost a bit more and offer no sticky objective shenanigans.

The Mission: Take and Hold Mirror

I'm going second on this one so I wait for Clay to move out on his first turn - he puts his Terminators too far forward and holds his Defiler back, while moving his Obliterators up. Deploying the Obliterators isn't the best move here, but he just didn't realize they only move 4" and that's a mistake I've seen before. They're just too slow to walk anywhere.

So I do what I do best and crash into him - I advance and Charge Bile and his unit of Chosen and Huron and his unit, killing the entire unit of Terminators and the Sorcerer without breaking a sweat. Meanwhile, the Nurglings move into position to help with the Defiler - the plan is for them to intervene and give it -1 to hit - and the Raiders make short work of the Traitor Guardsmen and get stuck in with the Obliterators. The Oblits can punch hard, but they'd rather be shooting and so keeping them fighting is a win.

Clay brings out his Defiler and loses it on the following turn, but makes a good push from my right flank with the Beastmen and Kravek Morne and his guys, making a scoring push  but failing their charge attempts. I had put my Vindicator back into reserves during deployment and used the opportunity to bring it in and shoot them, whittling the unit down so I could finish it off the following turn.

The Mutilators did manage to kill the Land Raider, but by the the time the final Terminator unit dropped Clay didn't have many options left and I threw Terminators + Legionaries + bikers at it to finish it off.

Result: 97-20, Win

Clay was a fun opponent and relatively new to the game - it's always rough to body someone in games like this but we had a good time and I think he learned a lot. I gave him some feedback after the game about using his reactive moves more and being more aggressive with the Defiler - he really put himself in a position to be alpha struck and it cost him.

Round 3: vs. Jeff Murphy's Tyranids

The final round was into Jeff's Tyranids, running Reconnaissance with the Ambush Predators and Vanguard Onslaught Detachments. His army was a Swarmlord, Tyrannofex, Winged Hive Tyrant, Biovore, Norn Assimilator, Genestealers + Broodlord, Hormagaunts, Raveners + Ravener Prime, two Neurolictors, Deathleaper, and a unit of Zoanthropes with a Neurotyrant.

The Mission: Purge and Secure vs. Reconnaissance Sweep

I started this one by using my Nurglings and Raiders' Infiltrators deployment to box Jeff in his deployment zone, then pulled them back using my Redeploy from the Masters of the Maelstrom. That kept Jeff from pushing too far forward, too fast. I was going second, which meant I could let him step forward tentatively and punish him.

This game was really about how nasty bolters are now and how annoying Nurglings can be. I pulled my Raiders forward with bikes on turn 1 and killed most of the Genestealers with shooting and a charge from the Raiders, and I used the Nurglings to tie up the Genestealers and keep the Raiders alive with the -1 to hit. The Norn intervened into the Genestealers and well, it spent two turns not killing them before my Vindicator and Land Raider shot it to death before it could ever reach the middle objective for its feel no pain.

I got super lucky in this one with my charges on round 2, making a series of 7/8-inch charges to tie up Jeff's units and keep things in my favor. I ended up pushing him back all game and using bolters to just blow large holes in a number of his units. S6 shooting from bolters is very nasty, and the ability to just plow forward and drop 20-30 shots at a time on enemy units with Letha/Sustained hits and full re-rolls made chewing through even bigger targets easy.

Jeff surveying the damage

This was another fun one but it was a bloodbath. At one point Jeff dropped his Raveners down near my Chosen brick and asked aloud "how much damage could they take in shooting?" and I could practically hear the Curb Your Enthusiasm theme start playing in my head. We had some fun moments with it despite the bloodbath however.

Result: 100-30, Win

Well, that set me to 2-1 and I did in fact win best painted. Jeff and Clay were great sports and I appreciated them both playing brutal games and keeping good spirits throughout. That's never easy.

Jeff had a lovely army, by the way - if you want to check out his work, he has an Instagram page where he shows off his painting and does commissions. Cool stuff.

Final Thoughts

That does it for this week - it was great to get in some practice games and I feel good about this as a Grand Narrative list, at least - walloping inexperienced players and medium lists while getting bodied by top meta lists feels like the area I want to shoot for most of the time, and I'll have some extra treats to add so I can scale up or down depending on need. Now it's just time to get a bunch of painting done.

See you next Thursday.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Historicals: SAGA Listbuilding Essentials
content:
We’ve finally convinced you to start playing SAGA, right? Now, instead of 2,500 points of army and dozens of units, you’re looking at 60+ different armies, usually four unit types and a grand total of six points to spend. Sounds simple, but once you dive in there’s a complex but masterable system at play. Let’s have a look at some SAGA list building essentials ranging from the very first steps all the way through to some deployment shenanigans.

Points and Army Size

Saga, like a huge number of other games, is a point buy system. You get between 4 and 8 points to spend, and allocate that spend to different units. All normal so far! A point always buys you a set number of models depending on the unit type. That means that usually a Saga army will be between 4-6 units in size. The most straightforward unit types are also straightforward with their sizes:

  • Hearthguard: Four models
  • Warriors: Eight models
  • Levy: 12 models

So 1 point can buy you four Hearthguard or eight Warriors or 12 Levy. This doesn't change with equipment. Eight Warriors with bows and on horses cost a point, as do eight warriors on foot with no additional equipment. Equipment choices are reflected in unit stats, not points cost.

One point of Warriors - eight models. Saga warbands clash for an unspecified reason

Your Warlord - again, regardless of equipment - is always free. This puts a lower and upper bound on the size of a Saga army.

Smallest Possible*

Warlord

Six points of Hearthguard (24 models)

Largest Possible

Warlord

Six points of Levy (72 models)

The first essential tip in this article is that both of these forces would be a bad choice in the vast majority of armies! Very few SAGA factions are set up to take advantage of all-hearthguard or all-levy.

*Smallest possible with the three base unit types - we’ll get onto the others eventually!

Four, Six, or Eight Points?

A four point game is a good starting point to get your head around the battleboards and start your army. It’s the lowest points level where the game functions as designed, and a four point play experience is still very satisfying. Starter 4 point lists tend to work the same way - one unit of each core type, with a point left over to tailor your list to your faction. This points level is quick, enjoyable and can almost certainly be made from virtually any historicals box you can buy provided it has - at minimum - 24 models in it.

A six point saga army. Credit: Mugginns.

The standard SAGA game size is six points, which allows for a nicely chunky board presence and lets you take a variety of units. Six point armies tend to be variable - enough points to buy the standards (see below), while tailoring your army to your faction board and play style. Playing at this points level is SAGA as designed, the ideal balance between complexity and playability, so always aim for six points!

Eight points is - mostly - reserved for Age of Magic, SAGA’s fantasy expansion. Age of Magic has a much wider variety of unit types and adds a magic system, so larger battles allow you to explore much more of what it has to offer. Eight points is also a good place to end up for other ages - not that you’re taking eight points of units, but that you’re painting and probably transporting eight points to events, giving you some flexibility for your list building by game. We’ll talk more about that later on!

Choosing Equipment

There are some basic suggestions that are worth following as you start out that will shape your armies. Equipment is reflected in Saga unit stats, so very briefly we can say:

  • Mounted: Faster but extra vulnerable to shooting.
  • Ranged weapons: Can shoot but are extra vulnerable to melee.
  • Heavy weapons: Hit harder in combat but are hit harder in return.

Generally, armour levels tend to vary by unit type. The basic rule of thumb is that Hearthguard are armour 5, warriors are 4, and levy are 3.

With these two points in mind, a basic starter saga army shouldn’t go too heavily into any one area. A shooting heavy army is extra vulnerable to melee, a mounted one to ranged attacks, a mounted AND ranged one is vulnerable to both.

Nearly all mounted - not always the best choice. My saracens in action.

Good advice to start out with would be:

  • Always take minimum one ranged unit if you can.
  • Dont load up on (3+ units) ranged unless your board has a lot of support for it.
  • Minimum one mounted unit if you can.
  • Always bring some infantry.

This gives you some shooting, some speed and the resilience of infantry units, and flexing up to two or three units of any one type allows you to specialise without putting all your eggs in one basket.

Once you know your army board, go crazy - my Saracens are all mounted with bows, and get shot to hell constantly.

Swapping Out

The choices aren’t over once you’ve spent your points. Unit sizes and equipment in saga are set on deployment, not on list writing, which gives you a huge range of flexibility between deciding what your point spend is and what hits the table. We’ll go into both unit sizes and equipment in more detail, but the important thing to remember is that you aren’t committed until you know the army your opponent is using and, depending on scenario, it’s possible that you can see some or all of their deployment before you decide!

That means you should know what good options are before you put a unit down. Two points of warriors can be deployed in multiple ways (see below), and units can be flexibly mounted or armed depending on your scenario and opponent.

Unit Sizes

There’s a key difference between SAGA and many other point buy systems, where your points aren’t buying you units but a certain number of models. You then split those models up into units of the same type. Two points of Warriors buys you 16 - which can be two units of eight, or, for example one unit of 10 and one of six.

The vast majority of SAGA units have to be between four and 12 models, so there are simple limits on your ability to chop and change your unit sizes. You can’t split a point of Hearthguard, for example, into two units of two. Likewise, you can’t combine every one of your 72 potential levy into one massive unit. Some larger models - elephants, cannons etc - can be deployed in units of one model.

Both of these units are a single SAGA point - Elephant and 12 levy. Credit: lenoon

Why bother? The answer is to balance SAGA Dice with unit effectiveness. Units generate dice for you to activate your faction abilities based on their size. Larger units shoot and fight better than smaller ones, though smaller ones may be easier to take through gaps in terrain. A unit of ten warriors hits harder - and survives longer - than a unit of 8. Let’s take two points of Warriors as an example, with three ways of allocating them. Each has advantages and disadvantages:

  • The larger the unit, the better it is in combat/shooting.
  • Larger units can absorb more casualties.
  • Smaller units are easier to move through terrain.
  • Multiple small units can make use of certain battle board abilities.
  • Units grant a SAGA dice at above minimum sizes.

So 16 warriors can be deployed as 2x8 warriors, 10 warriors and six warriors, 12 and four, or any variations between.

Why a Unit of 10?

A unit of 10 fights just a bit better than a unit of eight, and is a good place to put a war banner. Banners reduce your aggression (fighting dice rolled) to 0 for a single model, so a slightly larger unit allows you to have a banner while still chucking out a good amount of dice.

Why a Unit of Four?

Those four-model warrior units can still - in a pinch fight and shoot, but crucially they still generate a saga dice. Hearthguard always do, but warriors and levy only generate them above half strength (four and six models respectively). While you can only have a maximum of eight dice, you can absolutely sacrifice four warriors to a passive game in some terrain to get up to the cap.

A four model Hearthguard unit. Ok in combat, rubbish at staying at the back of the board generating a SAGA dice. get them fighting! Guy back left is clearly compensating for something with an extra large spear

Four model units are very vulnerable, but sat at the back, tucked into terrain and left all game they provide an extra saga dice while your other units do the fighting. This is a real mainstay of event SAGA play, though look out for the lesser seen variant of six ranged levy!

A good rule of thumb is that the more ranged or mounted units your enemies have, the larger your units should be. Multiple units of four warriors, while generating a lot of saga dice, are horribly vulnerable to shooting - a single casualty and they stop giving you that precious dice - and will fold almost immediately in combat. If you’re sitting down to play against a long ranged board (like the English in Age of Chivalry), multiple small units will get picked off very quickly. Boards where mobility is low and ranged troops are limited or absent (Vikings in Age of Invasions) will give you plenty of opportunity to sit a 4 man unit right at the back, untroubled all game.

Swapping Equipment

Swapping unit sizes as you deploy is big brained, but galaxy brain play is to swap out your equipment. Any saga unit that can be taken with options can change those options on deployment.

Most commonly this happens with warriors where several options crop up in many armies:

  • Mounted/on foot.
  • Ranged options - javelins, crossbows, slings, bows.
  • Special kit - pikes, sarissas, heavy weapons.

This also interacts with your unit sizes, so you can split two points of warriors into 12 mounted and four on foot if that’s an option for you. Again, you want to base this on your board, your opponent and your scenario. Let’s use my Saracens and two points of warriors as an example.

Saracens can take Mounted, foot, and mounted with bow warriors.

The board supports mounted and bow wielding warriors, so my base position is that I’ll take both.

One point of warriors on foot. Credit: Lenoon

I’m playing against Vikings - no real ranged threat and all on foot. Warriors go mounted with bows - I can shoot and scoot with almost total impunity without worrying about my warriors being armour 3 against shooting. I want some long-ranged charge threats too, so I’ll split a point into mounted without bows for a combat edge.

One point of warriors mounted with composite bows. Credit: Lenoon

I’m playing a scenario that requires me to enter terrain - four warriors go on foot so they don't pick up additional fatigue when in terrain.

The split - one point of warriors, half on foot and half mounted. Credit: Lenoon

My two points of warriors split into:

  • Eight mounted with composite bows
  • Four mounted
  • Four on foot

This gives me split that suits my board, plays well into my opponent’s army and can play the scenario too. This is where painting more than 6 points comes in handy - I have enough cavalry and composite bow warriors to switch the 4 points I usually spend on warriors between the three options should it be necessary.

Half Points

The point system is quick and easy to get used to, but can be a bit of a blunt instrument. What happens if you only want 12 warriors, and you don’t want to buy two points and split them into unequal units? Half points!

Half points are straightforward but occasionally worded in a confusing manner. You’ll see wording like “can be exchanged for two hearthguard, four warriors or six levy,” which essentially means “costs ½ a point”. You see this wording most frequently on larger unusual units like chariots or manubalistas, and the principle has been extended to all units.

Here's a half point of hearthguard providing a 6 model mounted threat. A Saga Game in full swing. Credit: Lenoon

Half points let you bulk up units without over investing in a particular unit type.

Hearthguard are the most common place people take half units - four hearthguard don’t always do that much, 8 hearthguard represent too many points in too few models, but six hits the sweet spot.

Consider half points for Warrior units where they have access to special equipment - composite bows, crossbows, chariots or sarissas - where you may not want to put all your eggs in one equipment basket

Levy half points can be used to add a small ranged unit or saga battery to stick in terrain, but both options are very vulnerable!

Top Tips and Tricks

Thracian Warband (Credit: paintbrush.mongrel)

That’s a lot, isn't it? Let’s boil it down to our top list building tips to start building Saga armies:

  • Always consider what your board is good at before you load up on a particular unit type.
  • Take a range of different unit types.
  • One mounted and one ranged is a good initial place to start.
  • You spend points in list building - you decide equipment and unit sizes at deployment.
  • Think flexibly about your unit sizes.
  • Tailor your equipment to your board, opponent and scenario.

Stick with these for your first couple of games and you won't go too far wrong - once you know your army (or armies, come on, may as well get more than one when your first costs all of about 30 quid), the SAGA world is your oyster. There's a huge variety of armies out there that can all do interesting things with unit sizes, equipment and variety, so get out and experiment!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: [Kill Team] Tactical Focus: Deployment 101
content:
It’s easy to overlook deployment in almost any tabletop game. I doubt that anyone is eagerly bounding over to a table because they simply cannot wait to take their dudes out of a case and place them on a board in the just right formation. Folks play tabletop wargames for the battles, the pretend war, the tiny plastic glory to be earned by rolling dice and pushing models around a board. For many players, especially those just starting out, deployment is just the act of setting up for the good stuff to follow.

Deployment isn’t the sexiest part of a game in any system, but an early lesson that most people learn early on is that no matter the system, deployment is one of the most important parts of any game. While good deployment rarely can win you a game all on its own, bad deployment can absolutely lose you a game before the very first turn. The key to winning any game is making sure your models are where they need to be on the board, when they need to be there, and poor deployment makes it all that much harder for you to do that. Poor deployment means you’ll waste time getting your forces to where they actually need to be on the board, all while key moments that you could’ve taken advantage of slip through your fingers.

Credit: Games Workshop

Kill Team is no different then any of these systems, and in some cases good deployment versus bad deployment can be even more pivotal than in many larger games since you have a much smaller number of models on the board to cover space. The last thing you want to realize in the middle of a match is that your operative with the nasty gun ended up somewhere on the board where they’ll never get the chance to shoot at a good target because they were deployed badly, and you didn’t figure it out until it’s too late.

So what are the best practices for good deployment in Kill Team? In this article, we’ll take a dive into a four step thought process behind building a strong and consistent plan for deploying your team on the table to help you better understand and improve your gameplan, and set yourself up to win in the Killzone before the first round even starts.

Necron Canoptek Circle Kill Team. Credit: Magos Sockbert

Step One: Know Your Team

In theory, Kill Team is a game with a limited number of variables for building a deployment plan. Especially if using the Approved Ops ruleset, there’s only so many maps to play on, and only so many teams you could expect to play against. You could, given enough time, patience, and practice, learn each and every matchup and map and build a tailor made plan for each combination. In practice, that’s a huge number of potential matchups, which doubles in size when you realize you factor in that your plan might change depending on which side of the killzone you’re deploying on, and then multiply that further when you take into consideration the different crit ops and tac ops. While some players can plan for each and every possibility, for most it’s impractical to plan for each individually. While there are a few important things to think about for the opponents team, such as considering their most dangerous operatives and their team’s threat ranges, the most important part of deployment is understanding your own team's rules, and having a general game plan before deployment even starts.

Knowing your own rules is important to winning sounds like I’m stating the obvious, but just because it’s low hanging fruit doesn’t make it any less true. There’s a pretty substantial number of teams in the game, even with declassified rotating out older teams from competitive play, and it’s almost a guarantee that most players won’t remember every single rule for teams they don’t regularly play as or against. You, on the other hand, are a fixed variable: you know exactly what team you’re going to be playing, you control that. So, learn your team’s rules, look it over and learn what the team is good at and bad at. If you know your teams rules like the back of your hand, then thats quite literally half the battle of knowing what the teams on the killzone do.

Plus, once you know your rules, you can understand what your team is good at, and from there you can start to build a plan on how to win. Is your team tough and good at bullying enemy operatives off objectives? Do you play your Tac Ops extremely well? Are you an all gas no brakes Kill Op team? How's your mobility? What offensive tricks do you have? Can you swarm your opponent with bodies, or are you an elite team who needs to be more careful with each operative? While it is true that no plan survives first contact fully intact, it’s important to have a general idea of what your path to victory in a game will look like, as well as maybe a handful of alternate plans in case you end up with a matchup that makes plan A difficult to do.

If you feel comfortable and confident in your own knowledge, and have a solid basic gameplan, it hugely reduces the mental load during both deployment and the game in general. You can worry more about how your plan is changing as the game goes on, rather than trying to decide what the plan is on the fly, which is a huge relief from the mental load during a game. Plus, generally these kinds of plans that are prepared for pre-game are much more difficult for an opponent to stop than something improvised haphazardly, even if that pregame plan is fairly loose.

Credit: Dan "Swiftblade" Richardson

Let’s take Murderwing, a team I’ve been playing extensively recently, as an example. I know that while this team has operatives that hit like a runaway freight train, it also has very limited defensive options and can lose operatives quickly if they’re hung out to dry, so generally I want to avoid just full sending the team unless I’m certain I can just overwhelm my opponent in a wall of Chaos Space Marine muscle. Because Murderwing is so mobile though, and I have great access to stuns and modifying APL, Murderwing can play the Crit Op and Tac Op fairly well, and thanks to Boost the team is super mobile and I can afford to hang back from objectives until I can zoom up and contest it safely. With this in mind, my general gameplan is to focus on Tac Op as my primary with Retrieval from Approved Ops 2025, and then focus on two objectives that I can stage safely far away from until I can fly up and take them near the end of a turning point. As a kicker, I can even send one operative on a long bomb run to the opponent home objective if I can get the right angle, which makes leaning on Retrieval even better. If I don’t think retrieval is going to work, I can pivot to Flank and use boost to reach safe spots in my opponents territory while picking off anyone sent my way, or Dominate if I can just get away with raking up kills in the back half of a game.

So without even seeing what map I’m playing on, or what team I’m up against, I’ve got the foundations of a gameplan and a path to how I will win. I’ll need to adjust for the unexpected of course, and there will always be the unexpected, but now when it's time to deploy I have a much better idea of where I need to place operatives so that they can be where they need to to execute the plan.

Step Two: Understand the Killzone

The next step in leveling up your deployment game is by understanding the various killzone maps in Kill Team, particularly in the Approved Ops mission pack.

While every Killzone will present a different set of problems and opportunities for your team, such as whether it’s open or close quarters and what sort of terrain and cover is nearby your drop zone, the main thing we’re going to focus on is what makes them all the same, and that’s how each Killzone can functionally be divided into three lanes based on where the objectives are placed on the map. Generally, if you take a look at any given Killzone and then split it into thirds based on where the objectives are placed, extending from drop zone to drop zone, these lanes become pretty easy to parse visually, even if they aren’t officially marked off from one another in any way.

While moving in between these three lanes can be very fluid in most games of Kill Team, during deployment it's important to decide how much you want to or need to control each of these lanes and deploy accordingly. Deciding to focus your efforts on controlling certain lanes tends to be a much more effective strategy than trying to spread your team out to be everywhere on the board at once, as it prevents you from being spread too thin and feeds back into your general game plan that you make prior to the start of the game.

As an example, if you know that you’re playing a team that wants to push aggressively into enemy territory, such as Vespid, it might be best to focus your deployment on the lane containing your opponents objective, where you’re likely to deliver the most pressure, while a smaller contingent of your forces hold the center and home objective lanes. For a team that wants to lie in wait, like Nemesis Claw, it may be best to ignore your opponent’s objective lane altogether and split your team between your home and center. While how your allocate your forces between each map may change based on the layout, understanding how to best split your team during deployment based on these three lanes will almost always be better than haphazardly trying to cover the whole board.

Step Three: Deploy Effective Equipment

Kill Team Volkus Terrain painted by Crab-stuffed Mushrooms

One of the most unique aspects of Kill Team is equipment selection and how it can shape your team by providing a wide toolbox of options for every team to draw upon that can change from game to game. While there's a good bit of equipment that doesn’t affect deployment choices at all, many pieces of equipment, such as barricades, mines, and razorwire, can be deployed on the killzone prior to the start of the game. In many cases, effective deployment of equipment can be just as important as effective deployment of your operatives.

When boiled down to its most basic functions, deployable equipment generally has one of two purposes (though some pieces can be used for either option): The equipment either protects or aids your operatives, or the equipment denies or debuffs your opponent. Based on what you need each equipment piece to do, you’ll need to consider the placement of each piece differently, but either way you’ll once again want to think about killzone lanes.

Buffing or aiding your team can come in several different forms, such as a barricade to protect your models from shooting, a ladder to help get your model traverse vantage quickly, a comms device to boost support abilities, or an ammo cache to buff your shooting reliability. Deciding where these equipment choices need to go is usually pretty easy, as it largely depends on where you want your operatives to be. While that does again seem like a very silly and obvious statement to make, considering which lanes you want your team to focus on controlling during a game and deploying buff equipment in these areas means you’ll make the most out of where you place items like a comms device, or get the most protection out of a barricade. It's also important to think about how you want to stage up the board for later turning points with these equipment options, making it easier to project threat in parts of the killzone you want to control while making it difficult for the opponent to threaten you.

As an example, a barricade placed right on the center objective is strong, especially if it’s out in the open against shooting, but it might be so far forward that making the best use of it puts you in easy threat range of enemy operatives. Placing a barricade further back from the objective while keeping it in your operatives effective threat range, whether it’s shooting or charging, means that if your opponent wants to control the center objective, they have to walk within your threat range, and now you’re the one who can effectively start a trade from a safe staging position.  Consider what lanes and objectives you want to control, and how these choices will help improve your control over that part of the board.

The other function of deployable equipment can be trickier, but just as effective, and that's using deployable terrain as area denial. Deployable equipment used as denial pieces strengthens your control over a given lane by making it more difficult for your opponent to access it freely, slowing them down or corralling them into specific areas of the map. Examples of universal equipment choices that can do this include mines, razorwire, and even barricades placed at choke points that your enemy has to spend movement trying to climb. As far as where this denial equipment is usually most effective, they tend to be most effective in spots that either deny access to your home objective, or at choke points between lanes that make it difficult for your opponent to move freely from one lane to another should they have to redirect their forces. If there’s a part of the map you know you don’t want your opponent to be, and think your opponent will be able to easily get there if left unchecked, consider using deployable equipment options at those spots to slow down or deny your opponent access altogether.

Brood Brothers Kill Team. Credit: John from Can You Roll A Crit?

Step Four: Deploy Effective Operatives

A little over two thousand words later, and we’re finally on how we can best deploy our operatives.

After all of the considerations we’ve made so far, actually getting down to deploying our operatives might just be the easiest part here, since every decision we’ve made so far has set us up for success. We know what our path to winning the game looks like, we know what areas of the killzone we need to control to do it are, and we’ve set up our equipment to either improve our strength in a lane or deny the opponent free access. Every choice here has brought us to a razor sharp point that shows exactly where we need to be, which means when we’re deploying our team, we’re not just improvising or putting down operatives wherever. We can be purposeful in our decision, and maximize the effectiveness of our team.

The most important part of deployment, plan or no plan though, is to place your operatives in safe parts of your drop zone. This takes priority over all else, even if it means splitting your forces up more than you may like. An operative is no good to you if your opponent can grab an easy shot on it. If your safe spots are truly dire, consider using equipment to buy you more safe real estate in your drop zone.

Feral Mechanicum Kill Team; Credit: Colin Ward

Being purposeful is the key aspect here, and even if we’ve set up for success already, we still need to think on a per operative basis on where they will be most effective. For example, if you have an operative with a key support ability that improves your team’s offensive or defensive capabilities, they need to be deployed where you expect the bulk of your team to be, which means that this operative probably isn’t one you want babysitting your home objective. Or if you have a very aggressive operative, they need to be placed somewhere where you plan on the bulk of the engagement to be, as the last thing you want is to waste precious time trying to redeploy them because they were deployed too far away from the action.

Lastly, a good rule of thumb for deployment is think about where you want your models to be at the end of turning point one, and then set your model up in a spot where they can reach that part of the killzone when they activate. In the current edition of Kill team, turning point one doesn’t present any ability for your team to score outside of kill op, which almost always requires you to overextend your model, so that first turning point move is almost like a secondary deployment for the following three turning points. Just like with deployment, rather than just pushing your operatives directly up the board absentmindedly on the first turn, consider where you need to be to score points according to your game plan, and reposition your operatives in a spot to do so, even if it means potentially having a model not leave the drop zone so that it can be more effective later in the game. No matter where the operative needs to go that first turn though, the only way they can reach it is if they’re deployed in the right spot.

Credit: Dan "Swiftblade" Richardson

Final Thoughts

Deployment is the least interactive part of Kill Team, and while your opponents placement may influence your own placement of operatives and equipment, there's no randomness from the dice involved in deployment and no conflict to consider. It is entirely an operation that you, the player, control, and because of that it's one of the most important parts of the game to have a plan for. As stated earlier in the article, while deployment is something that very rarely wins a game all on its own, you can absolutely lose a game by deploying poorly before any dice are ever rolled. Deployment is the foundation for the rest of your game to follow, and with a carefully considered plan to build from and by deciding what lanes of the Killzone you need to focus your efforts on, it's much easier to set your equipment and operatives in positions to execute that strategy effectively and set yourself up to be in the strongest position possible for the rest of the match.

title: [Warmachine] Competitive Innovations in the Iron Kingdoms: WTC, Lock & Load, and the End of 2026 Meta
content:
The end of the Warmachine event year is defined by two events:

  • Warmachine WTC (World Teams Championship)
  • Lock & Load US (Premier Steamforged Games run end of year Iron Gauntlet)

While drastically different approaches are required for both formats, they equally encourage the best of the best to hone what has emerged as the top of the meta. The sea of releases this year has certainly been a challenge for top tournament players to navigate but some clear winners did emerge.

Credit: Steamforged Games

World Team Championship 2026

First was WTC, the global showcase of skill and prowess from countries across continents with several countries bringing multiple teams. Going into the event the obvious meta front runners were Grymkin, Old Umbrey, and the new meta powerhouse Fane of Nyrro. As such it was assumed they would dominate the overall meta representation, which was remarkably not the case.

Outside of Thornfall Alliance and other Armies of Legend whose results are statistically insignificant, the most popular armies at WTC, Old Umbrey and Wicked Harvest, demonstrated why they were taken so often as they put up solid win rates despite being known quantities that define the metagame, although their win rates were not out of bounds. The other big winners were Brineblood Marauders, Orgoth Sea Raiders and Dark Operations, all of which certainly outperformed the win rates of several more popular armies. These armies were probably very well positioned to fight into the established metagame and carve success out of a crowded field where the more popular armies could be easily predicted. These are also older armies often piloted by dedicated players, so there can easily be something of an experience difference compared to the newer, more popular armies, particularly in cases where the pilots of the newer armies were not as well-practiced into the likes of Dark Operations or Sea Raiders, allowing them to submarine into impressive performances despite their small caster stables.

The biggest losers, win rate-wise, were House Kallyss, Gravediggers and Winter Korps. Gravediggers and Winter Korps have a very gun-focused army plan in a meta dominated by Morosov and Old Witch and thus very hostile into shooting. They also currently demonstrate limited caster variety based on how much Baranov and Cyn were in the field, which made them easier to plan for than armies with a wider stable of viable casters. The popularity of House Kallyss was probably the biggest surprise of the WTC statistics, but those were mostly dominated by Tyrus/Hellyth pairings. Although the pairing was strong and can be successful (as discussed later), it ended up being another known quantity that had questionable success into the major bogeymen armies of the event.

Credit: Steamforged Games

Fane of Nyrro was probably the biggest surprise in terms of expectations vs reality of their popularity and success rate, as many predicted that they would be the most popular and dominating faction of the event, but there are a couple of asterisks to this point. The first being that Fane did not have all of their in-app tools available. Harasheth was a legal model due to his Warmachine 3D version, but the rest of his box was not, and getting access to powerful models like the Riven and Styrge Hounds would have certainly changed the game. The other asterisk is that Nymara, as a caster, had an absurdly strong 67% win rate, with the dismal performance of the other Fane casters bringing the overall stats into the realm of reasonable. Nymara was a popular and powerful choice throughout both of the year’s capstone events and is absolutely a caster to watch.

The winning team, Australia Charging Cassowaries, had an eclectic mix of armies, being one of the rare teams to double up on their factions with two House Kallyss players as well as Grymkin, Old Umbrey and Winter Korps. The off-meta choices continue into the individual list choices as the Grymkin pairing does not contain Old Witch and although Morosov and Lissya were common sights at the event, both those lists have unique spins with Lissya’s extra-heavy cohort build and Morosov’s shifters heavily favoring werewolves over the more common werebears.

The pairing process and performance of the winners indicates that the Cassowaries were well aware of the meta and made their choices deliberately to counter the expected meta. Perhaps the most pronounced examples of this are the double Dusk lists. Hazaroth seems to have explicitly been the Fane of Nyrro drop as Hazaroth was played into it 3 times and going 2-1, while Dan Tacken’s Hellyth list came loaded for bear with an impressive 4 drops into Old Umbrey, going 3-1 in that matchup. The wolf-heavy Morosov list appears to have been built for Grymkin, dropping into Old Witch twice. Finally, Robin de Oliveira’s Heretic/King of Nothing pairing must have presented significant pairing challenges for all of the Grymkin drops that were mostly prepared for Old Witch, going 5-0 and taking the coveted number 2 spot on the individual players list. Although the list has no bearing on the results and shouldn’t be used as a pure indication of player skill given the WTC matchup process, it’s still very impressive for a list with 240 names on it.

Lock and Load US

Lock & Load US is characterized by the now legendary Iron Gauntlet which people have been qualifying for throughout the year at their local aptly named Iron Gauntlet Qualifiers. The format is an iron man event, which is to say players are separated into pods and those pods feed their top players into a final single elimination event where winner takes all.

Out of the 32 qualified players who decided to attend we see a fairly warped trend of stats. Players of this skill level made a true mix of understandable and baffling army choices. Was it just their own personal comfort pick? A back pocket favorite to have fun with? The deliberate attempt to attack this brutal gauntlet with a dark horse choice? Let's dig in and find out!

Dread Armada were obviously the breakout stars, with four players (including the ultimate winner) getting an army printed out in the scant week between the files going live and Lock and Load happening. Wicked Harvest, Gravediggers and especially Fane of Nyrro, now in possession of all of their tools except those announced at the event itself, made up fully half of the top 32, with the others split fairly evenly between most of the other factions and a few Armies of Legend to keep things interesting. Notable at this level is the complete absence of Sea Raiders or Shadowflame Shard as representatives of the wholly new armies released since the start of Mk4. Although none of the Gravediggers players advanced, which was predictable based on their poor performance at the WTC, the Wicked Harvest going 0 for 4 into the top 16 was a bit surprising, but there is a reason for this.

Credit: Steamforged Games

Interestingly, the meta that so defined the WTC team formation and results appears largely absent in the top 16 of the Iron Gauntlet. By contrast, several of the armies on display are either very new (Dread Armada, Fane including new post-WTC models such as the Styrge Hounds and Styrge Abhorreth) or are older armies of legend that are bringing their classic tools to bear in the current game (Devourer’s Host, Ravens of War). It appears that, taking some lessons from WTC about the risks of playing into a predictable meta, several of the players instead opted to try and ambush opponents with options that opponents may not have had the opportunity or time to practice against, leading to a lot of improvisational decision making. When expecting a single elimination format, forcing your opponent to think even more about what you have brought is a valuable edge.

While the broader meta is split between newer and much older armies, the top end of the of the meta seems to be defined by front-line personal work casters, with Terminus, Nymara and Dekathus all dominating the top end and Vorsalys being a choice to try to keep those melee monsters in check. By contrast, more back-line casters like Shadowtongue, Vorgoroth, Vayl and Harasheth did not find corresponding success, all being defeated by the front-line powerhouses. It appears that Wicked Harvest was also fairly vulnerable to these powerful front-liners, whose aggressive play and innate resilience appeared to push the little nightmares out of the top cut. Combined with Old Witch being slated for a power reduction and the most successful Grymkin list at WTC being Witch-less, it will be interesting to see how Grymkin builds will adjust into 2027.

The final match was a battle of the new stuff, with the all new Dread Armada army led by Terminus and piloted by Dan Riker finding success against Peyton Preece’s Vorsalys, who was packing his own brand new toys in two Styrge Abhorreths (soon eager to try the even newer models revealed at the event itself to be sure). The combination of Entropic Shroud and Aegis in the Terminus list reducing most enemy spell ranges to effectively zero appears to be a big part of allowing Terminus to retain his threatening agency against a field where powerful control effects were common.

Image Credit: Steamforged Games

Warmachine in 2026 was one of the most tumultuous competitively. Between the official release of four full armies, the re-release of three more, and a rare mid-year update the overall meta felt like it was changing weekly. The armies and archetypes of gunlines and aggressive anti-gunlines were systematically replaced with aggressive mid board bullies that could play wide in sub-packages and silos. Spheres of control and combat around very widely spread out objectives. While exciting to learn about as new rules were revealed the added complications of new mechanics was exciting to many and suffocating to others. While Lock and load had some distinct surprises and the podium of WTC deviated from American expectations, many hope the 2027 meta is more stable. More armies that feel in line with the new SFG style of mechanics not simply propped up by highly skilled faction experts. Warmachine has been coming back with a vengeance, and as far as army updates/additions were concerned, 2026 was an explosion of accessibility, so we hope things even out with the new update so everyone can play this awesome game their way.

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.
